#8266. 10 Times Ted Lasso Totally Nailed This Whole Parenting Thing

Ted Lasso isn’t the perfect father, but he’s one who can teach us a thing... or 10.

Way back in 2020, when I heard that Apple TV was releasing a Ted Lasso show based on the NBC Sports English Premier League promo campaign of the same name, I dismissed the concept out of hand. Sure, I loved the cheeky ads where an American football coach goes to England to manage a football club. But the premise felt too thin to flesh out into a full series, and Jason Sudeikis’ body of work up to that point didn’t inspire confidence that a sitcom based on the character could hold my attention.

Here’s the thing I failed to anticipate: Ted Lasso is, at its core, a show about fatherhood. Not in a neat, Hallmark-movie kind of way, but in the messy, long-distance, guilt-soaked, love-you-so-much-it-hurts way that a lot of us actually live it. Ted’s relationship with his son, Henry — conducted mostly through grainy FaceTime calls across a six-hour time difference — is the quiet beating heart of all three seasons.

While the rest of AFC Richmond is arguing about formations and tabloid covers, Ted is trying to figure out how to be a good dad from 4,000 miles away while working through how his relationship with his own father has formed him.

The man is not perfect. Nobody raising kids is, and running off to London without your family to accept a job you’re wholly unqualified for as an act of emotional avoidance is a narrative necessity, but it’s a flaw many folks have pointed out.

But along the way, he does his best and makes the right plays in the moments that count. And since parenting lessons wrapped inside a feel-good soccer comedy are my personal favorite delivery mechanism, let’s run through 10 times Ted Lasso gave us a genuine master class in this whole dad thing.

It’s Ted’s first night in London. He’s jet-lagged and disoriented, and the very first thing he does is call home to Henry. He fumbles the time zones and sounds a little lost, but he makes sure his kid hears his voice before the day is out.

There’s a version of Ted Lasso in a different corner of the multiverse who gets swept up in the new job, the new city, the chaos of it all, and phones it in on the fatherhood front. This Ted doesn’t. He knows that presence isn’t always physical. Sometimes it’s a crackling FaceTime connection at midnight your time, 6 a.m. their time, just so your kid knows you’re still there.

Henry, during a video call, asks his dad if he’s ever run into The Beatles over there in England and whether he can get a photo with John, Paul, George, and Ringo. Now, Ted knows that both John Lennon and George Harrison have been dead for decades. He also knows his kid is 8 years old and asking with complete, genuine wonder. So Ted just agrees to try. He doesn't have the heart to kill that particular joy right now.

This one is subtle, but it matters. There's a real parenting skill in knowing when the truth can wait five minutes and when it needs to be delivered immediately. Ted isn't being dishonest — he's being developmentally attuned. There's a season for everything, as a certain king once sang from the stage of a Broadway house, and this particular season called for letting a little kid's imagination breathe. Ted will level with Henry about the hard stuff — and he does, plenty of times — but he picks his moments. That's wisdom.

When Michelle and Henry show up in London, Ted drops everything. They swing by the Crown and Anchor for an authentic English pub experience. They build a double-decker bus model at the kitchen table. And Henry settles into his happy place, sleeping between his parents. Even though Ted is in the midst of a brutal season, managing a locker room full of fragile egos while racking up losses, none of that matters for those few days. He is simply Dad.

What makes this moment rich is what we know that Henry doesn't: His parents' marriage is already over. Michelle is about to tell Ted she wants a divorce. And yet Ted keeps the joy intact for his son. He doesn't let his own grief occupy the visit. That is an act of real parenting discipline — the ability to compartmentalize your own pain long enough to give your child a memory that isn't shadowed by yours. Most of us have had to do some version of this. It doesn't feel heroic in the moment. It just feels hard. Ted does it anyway.

Henry asks Ted why, whenever he sees him on TV coaching soccer, he never seems to be doing anything. It's a kid's question, but it's actually a perfect question. Ted's answer is one of the most quietly profound things in the entire series. He tells Henry that once the game starts, he can't really tell his players what to do — he just has to hope that everything he's been trying to teach them made some kind of dent. Then he says: “It's kind of like being a father.”

And then Henry, having absorbed none of this, is clearly already thinking about something else entirely. Ted realizes midsentence that his kid has mentally bounced. He stops talking. He smiles. He gets it. That moment is the whole job description of parenthood distilled into 30 seconds of television. You pour yourself into the role and hope it lands. You accept that you can't control the outcome. And you find a way to laugh about it — or at least smile — when your kid demonstrates, in real time, that they were not listening. Every parent reading this has lived this exact moment.

Henry isn’t the first kid to idolize a less-than-stellar role model, but his admiration for Jamie Tartt is a particular form of torture for Ted. As enigmatic as he is talented, Jamie makes Ted’s life incredibly difficult, even when he’s scoring goals. This puts Ted in a tough spot as Henry enthusiastically belts out the terribly annoying Baby Shark-themed Jamie Tartt song and sports his jersey with pride.

But Ted lets his son revel in the moment of having access to the talented and popular starlet. He doesn’t even hint at the fact that perhaps Tartt isn’t the best guy to look up to. And when Jamie flashes Ted a smirk that makes his beautiful face even more punchable than usual while signing Henry’s jersey, Ted takes a deep breath and lets his son have a moment he’ll never forget.

Ted gets word from Michelle that Henry has been involved in a bullying situation at school — and then discovers it wasn't Henry who was bullied. Henry was the bully. Ted is shaken. And because of schedules and time zones, he has difficulty getting in touch with Henry right away.

If Ted had been around, he would likely have responded emotionally and sucked all the air out of the room. But when father and son finally get a chance to talk, Henry admits he messed up and didn't follow his dad's advice to count to 10 when he gets angry.

With a little bit of forced space, Henry comes back around on his own. Ted doesn't strip his son of dignity while correcting him. And when Henry apologizes to his friend Doug with a rap in front of the class, you can almost hear Ted beaming through the phone. The lesson Ted had been repeating wasn't wasted — it just needed more time to work. Be a goldfish, sure, but also trust that the seeds you plant eventually grow. Even in the hardest soil.

When Michelle and Henry leave London at the end of their visit, Ted walks them to the gate, knowing his marriage is essentially over and that his son doesn't know it. He says goodbye to Henry the way you say goodbye when you're not sure when you'll see each other again — fully present, holding it together, promising to talk soon. He watches Henry walk away with the airport attendant. And then the mask slips, just for a moment, and you see how much it costs him.

Here's what Ted doesn't do: He doesn't make the goodbye about himself. He doesn't get weepy in a way that burdens Henry with having to manage his father's emotions. He saves that for after the kid is out of sight. This is something parents don't talk about enough — the emotional labor of keeping your own grief off your child's plate. It's not suppression. It's protection. There's a version of this that's emotionally avoidant and unhealthy, but Ted's version in this moment is clear-eyed and loving. He feels everything. He just knows whose feelings need managing right now.

After Henry's visit to London ends and the lad heads back to Kansas, Ted does something small and wonderful. He shows Henry, via video call, that he's placed the miniature Premier League Lego trophy Henry gave him into the Nelson Road Stadium Lego set they built together. It's a tiny thing. It's also everything.

Physical objects carry emotional weight for kids in ways that words sometimes can't. That Lego stadium becomes a shared artifact. It’s something Henry can picture when he thinks of his dad. Something that says “you were here, and you matter, and I kept a piece of what we made.”

It's the parenting equivalent of keeping a drawing on the fridge forever. Henry even notices that Nate's Lego figure is at the back of the bench and asks about it, which gives Ted a gentle opening to explain that relationships can change without anyone being erased. Heavy stuff, delivered through the medium of tiny plastic soccer coaches.

During their Lego video call conversation, Ted tells Henry that he doesn't love the idea of being away from him and that the only reason he's staying in England is that he's doing something important. Henry — who is, let's remember, about 10 years old — tells his dad to try to win the whole thing. Ted pushes back, saying winning isn't everything. And Henry says, essentially: “OK, but at least try.”

That's the moment a kid flips the script on you, and you realize they've been absorbing your lessons all along and also developing their own perspective on top of them. Ted doesn't dismiss the advice. He doesn't say “thanks, buddy” in that patronizing way parents sometimes do. He actually sits with it. He lets Henry be right.

Kids need to see their parents receive feedback and adjust — it's how they learn that it's a normal and healthy thing to do. Plus, Henry is objectively correct. You can care about more than winning and still bring your whole effort to the field. That's not a contradiction. That's maturity.

Ted walks away from AFC Richmond. He turns down the job. He gets on the plane. He comes home to Kansas and, within about 60 seconds, is coaching Henry's junior league team, running plays, completely in his element.

But the real parenting lesson isn't just that Ted comes home. It's why he comes home. He doesn't do it because the job went badly or because England rejected him. He does it because he looked at his life clearly and made an honest accounting of what mattered most. He showed his son — showed Henry in the most concrete way possible — that he is the priority. Not in the abstract, inspirational-poster way. In the literal, I-quit-my-dream-job-in-London-to-be-at-your-soccer-games way.

And then in the finale's final image, when Henry misses a shot and gets frustrated, Ted calls him over. Henry says the words Ted has been saying all series — be a goldfish — and they both smile.

The lesson came back home. Same as the dad.

#8265. The Clever Way to Reuse Old Tomato Cages to Protect Your Plants From Freezing Temperatures

Your empty tomato cages can shelter tender shrubs from frost and snow all winter and help safeguard next summer's flowers.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Wrapped in frost cloth or burlap, an old tomato cage becomes a cheap but effective shelter to protect plants this winter. All sorts of tender shrubs and perennials need winter protection, and temporarily shielding even hardy plants from the worst of the weather can help them thrive. So if you're about to pack away your tomato cages in the shed, stop – they've got another job to do now it's time to winterize garden plants this fall.

Pulling up tomato plants and stacking their cages in the shed until spring is one of the last big gardening jobs of the season. That's a lot of good wire sitting around in the dark all winter, and this trick puts it right back to work. Most gardens have a plant or two that struggles through the cold months, and overwintering plants usually means spending money on shrub covers, frost tents or frames, or insulating zip-up plant jackets built for the job. None of it costs much alone, but the outlay adds up across a whole bed and your old cage can do much of that same work to winterize plants.

This trick won't save everything, but for the right plants a tomato cage wrapped in frost cloth or burlap is a smart, cheap way to help your garden get through winter unscathed. So, if you're gardening on a budget and wondering how to protect plants in winter, here's the smart solution.

Throw insulating fabric straight over a shrub and it settles right onto the leaves and buds, and cold will seep through wherever it touches. Wet snow is worse. Its weight can bend or snap branches under the cover. But put a tomato cage in there first and the fabric sits on the frame instead, with a little gap between cover and plant. This method also gives you a frame to fasten the fabric to so it stays put when the wind picks up.

Start with the cage itself. You'll probably find dried leaves and sections of vine still wound through the wire. If last summer's plants had Septoria leaf spot (Septoria lycopersici) or early blight (Alternaria solani), those scraps can carry it over, so pull every one out and disinfect by scrubbing the cage with diluted household bleach and a rinse.

Next comes the fit. Lower the clean cage over the plant and see where the branches end up. Any branch poking through the wire is, more or less, where the fabric will touch the plant later, so the stems need room inside. Push the legs down firmly and, out in an open, windy bed, tie it to a sturdy stake if needs be.

Now wrap the frame in breathable frost cloth or horticultural fleece: one Agfabric frost blanket, available from Home Depot, covers more than one cage. Fasten the fabric to the frame using clips like these stainless steel garden clips from Walmart. Take the fabric right down to the soil as warmth comes up out of the ground at night and a gap at the bottom lets it leak out. Pin the fabric to the ground with galvanized landscape staples like these from Walmart.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Skip plastic wrap, because the plant needs to breathe and a wrapped cage heats up fast on mild afternoons and damp, still air favors gray mold (Botrytis cinerea). Even without a waterproof wrap, peek underneath every few days and let some fresh air in if needs be. Once the cold snap is over, take the temporary covers off, leaving the frame in place ready for the next weather dip.

Depending on your USDA zone, the plants that need winterizing in fall aren't just those that aren't hardy enough to survive plummeting temperatures: you can use this trick to extend a crop or protect next year's flower show, too. Ever had a hydrangea leaf out nicely and then barely bloom? Bigleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea macrophylla) is the classic candidate because it forms next year's flower buds on old wood, and those buds sit on bare stems all winter. Hard freezes can kill these delicate buds so while the foliage comes through just fine the following year, blooms are few and far between.

Hybrid tea roses and perennials that are borderline hardy in your zone are good candidates too. If you've planted young shrubs this year – especially if you've been tempted by Black Friday sales on evergreen shrubs and you're planting late in fall – they'll also benefit from being kept cozy during cold snaps. Boxwood and other small evergreens can pick up winter burn from drying wind and sun, and burlap like this Wellco natural burlap roll at Home Depotcuts down on both without pressing on the foliage.

Of course, you'll need to match the plant to the cage size. But if you're planning to upgrade your tomato cages to use a more substantial modular tomato support set-up like these heavy-duty square tomato cages, also from Home Depot anyway, it makes sense to do so now when you can use them to protect bigger shrubs that need a wider frame.

Once the plant goes dormant, usually after several hard frosts, a sturdy cage can be packed with loose insulation to provide further insulation too. Dry shredded leaves, straw or pine straw like this from Amazon is best. On a bigleaf hydrangea, you can fill right up around the buds, while roses mostly need the extra insulation over the crown and lower canes.

Keep that fill dry and loose. Leaves raked off a wet lawn and packed tight against living foliage or a crown stay soggy, and that can lead to rot, so let them dry out first before covering with frost fabric. In spring, pull out the fill a little at a time once the worst cold has passed.

Frost cloth doesn't make any heat of its own, but only slows the loss of warmth rising from the ground at night, buying a few degrees on a clear, still night. In a long, deep freeze, the soil underneath cools off too, and that leaves the cover less and less to work with. Truly tropical plants won't turn winter-hardy inside a wrapped cage, either: hibiscus and mandevilla belong indoors once nights turn chilly, well ahead of frost. In colder regions, some tender plants on the edge of hardiness still do better potted up and stored in a frost-free spot.

For most of the year, a tomato cage has one job. But with a cozy comforter of frost cloth, a few clips and a bit of care, this garden staple picks up a second role in winter, sheltering plants that would otherwise need a store-bought cover and helping to ensure another flower-filled year in your garden. When spring comes, unwrap your precious plant, hose off the cage and send it back to the tomato bed. It's the same old cage pulling double duty, and this trick to reuse it over winter barely costs a dime.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#8264. Drinks You Can Make By The Batch

Bring something good. Let the grown-ups serve themselves.

Holiday magic is a lot of unpaid labor in an ugly Christmas sweater. Between class potlucks, Thanksgiving logistics and buying the only bread your kid will eat, you’ve got enough on your plate. Now add holiday parties, questionable white elephant gifts and 400 things to do before the doorbell rings. The last thing you need is a second job as a bartender.

These punches, pitchers and alcohol-free drinks are perfect for pre-plan prepping.There’s a spicy margarita you can carry in the tequila bottle, a pear punch for the fancy friends, and a peppermint espresso martini you can make for 16. Some need a little attention before serving. Most are ready to pour once chilled.

Julie Reiner, co-founder of Brooklyn’s Clover Club, served punch and freezer cocktails at a Halloween party for 20. “The goal is to spend time with your guests, not be stuck behind the bar all night!” she said.

A little planning helps. Julianna McIntosh, the cocktail creator behind Join Jules, recommends using fresh citrus the day of your party and accounting for the water normally added when you shake or stir a drink with ice. Hannah Chamberlain, the recipe developer behind Spirited LA, has another rule: Hold the ice and bubbly until guests arrive. Otherwise, you risk a watered-down punch with flat bubbles.

Bringing a batch to someone else’s party? Pack it in a tightly sealed container, keep it chilled and add the bubbles when you arrive. Then pour yourself a glass and let someone else worry about the rest.

Bitter, bubbly and ridiculously easy to scale up. Natalie Migliarini, the cocktail creator behind Beautiful Booze, makes her Negroni Sbagliato with equal parts Select Aperitivo, sweet vermouth and prosecco, finished with an orange slice. The recipe makes one, but you can multiply the aperitivo and vermouth to serve your group, then chill them together in a bottle. When it's time to drink, pour over ice, add the prosecco and stir. No shaker required.

Everyone’s due at six. The first guest rings the bell at 5:42. Have Reiner’s Boat House Punch ready. Gin, Aperol, St-Germain and three citrus juices get a bright, bittersweet lift from sparkling rosé. “I always want my punch to be a crowd-pleaser, but it needs to have a little personality too!” Reiner said. This makes a substantial batch, so save it for a crowd. Let the lemon peels and sugar sit for at least an hour or overnight, and freeze a large ice block ahead of time. Add the ice and rosé just before serving.

Champagne tastes even better when nobody has to mix 12 individual cocktails. Chamberlain's large-batch take on the French 75 combines gin, fresh lemon, orange bitters and homemade cranberry-ginger syrup, then gets topped with sparkling wine. It serves six to eight and looks impressive without requiring an elaborate garnish situation. Make the syrup ahead and chill the ingredients. When guests arrive, add large ice cubes and the bubbly, give it a stir, and you're done. If the finished punch tastes a little dull, Chamberlain recommends adding a few dashes of Angostura or cardamom bitters to give it more personality.

Love your friends. Not enough to muddle each of them a mojito. Averie Sunshine’s pomegranate mojito punch at Averie Cooks combines white rum, mint, pomegranate juice and seeds, lemon and sparkling water in one pitcher. It makes four generous drinks, so double it for a bigger gathering. Chill the liquids ahead, then muddle the mint and assemble the punch just before serving so the leaves stay fresh, and the bubbles don't disappear. Ice goes in the glasses. One round of muddling. Everybody gets a drink.

Here, Chamberlain pairs pear nectar with gin, ginger liqueur, rosemary syrup, lemon, cardamom bitters and dry bubbly in her Calling Card Punch. It's an elegant, herbal alternative to the usual holiday punch and serves six to eight. Make the rosemary syrup ahead, chill the ingredients and add the sparkling wine while serving.

“I tend to build my punch a little less sweet and then I’ll often have a little extra syrup I can add if it seems unbalanced,” Chamberlain said. It's easier to add sweetness than take it away.

By the time dessert rolls around, the adults deserve something stronger than another cup of coffee. McIntosh combines vodka, espresso or cold brew, coffee liqueur and peppermint syrup for a holiday spin on the espresso martini. Her large-batch version makes about 16 servings, with no individual shaking required. Mix everything ahead, chill it in the freezer for about two hours and give it a quick whirl in the blender if you want that signature foam. Pour into a punch bowl and let everyone help themselves. Crushed candy cane rims are optional. You've already done enough decorating.

Give the alcohol-free drinks their own spot at the party. America’s Test Kitchen combines cranberries, ginger, rosemary, cinnamon and star anise in a sweetened base you can make up to four days ahead. When guests arrive, add chilled cranberry juice, orange juice and seltzer. It makes 16 servings, enough for an open house where another family keeps appearing in the doorway.

Get the recipe at America’s Test Kitchen.

The tiny apple leaves are optional – you have enough crafts coming home from school. Chamberlain’s Fallen Leaves Punch mixes cognac, tart apple cider and lemon with homemade cranberry-cinnamon syrup for eight servings. It's a good Friendsgiving option if you want something tart, fruity and a little stronger than cider.

“In terms of flavor combinations, it’s hard to disappoint with the combination of seasonal spice and fruit,” Chamberlain said. Make the syrup ahead, squeeze the lemons the day of and stir everything over a large ice block at serving.

Taco night doesn’t need a November makeover. McIntosh makes six spicy margaritas right in the tequila bottle, giving you a batch and a carrying container in one. You'll need to pour out some tequila first; the recipe tells you how much. Mix everything in the bottle, then let it sit in the freezer for 2 to 4 hours, then pour it over ice into salt-rimmed glasses. All the fun of margaritas without anyone spending the evening squeezing limes.

Apple cider is doing a lot of heavy lifting this holiday season, let it have some rum. Chamberlain's Cider Rum Punch combines tart cider, aged pineapple rum, lemon, orange bitters and a homemade mulling-spice syrup for six servings. She makes it every year, and it's easy to see why. The warm spices play nicely with the fruit without turning the whole thing into a scented candle. Make the syrup ahead, then combine everything in a pitcher with plenty of ice and stir until chilled. Bonus: There's no sparkling wine to worry about going flat.

The kids’ table and Grandma can drink from the same pitcher. McIntosh’s pineapple passion fruit agua fresca blends tropical fruit, lime and agave into six refreshing alcohol-free servings. Frozen passion fruit pulp works, and there are no bubbles to go flat on the drive. Make it up to two days ahead, refrigerate and give it a good stir before pouring over ice.

After the holiday lights walk, everyone comes home freezing and suddenly needs something warm RIGHT NOW. Sunshine's peppermint white hot chocolate at Averie Cooks combines milk, melted white chocolate and a little peppermint extract. The recipe makes five mugs, but you can easily double or triple it for a houseful of cold kids and grown-ups. Heat everything together over low heat, stirring until the chocolate melts. Don't let it boil, and go easy on the peppermint. A little goes a long way. Add marshmallows if you've got them. Nobody's going to complain.

The wine people and the margarita people can share a pitcher. Migliarini’s tequila sangria at Beautiful Booze combines Sauvignon Blanc with tequila, cranberry syrup, fresh cranberries, red and green apples and lime. “Keeping it simple, my recipe includes fruits that are available throughout the entire year,” she writes in the recipe. It serves five to six, making it a good choice for a casual Friendsgiving. Chill the wine, tequila and fruit mixture ahead, then add the lemon-lime soda just before serving.

No fish. Promise. Amy Traynor’s Fish House Punch at Moody Mixologist combines cognac and aged rum with peach liqueur, lemon and cold black tea. Think peach iced tea with considerably more going on. Her recipe includes a version for 10, so there's no need to multiply or do any guesswork. Freeze a large ice block ahead, stir the ingredients over it at serving and finish each glass with freshly grated nutmeg. Fair warning: This one's boozy.

Dinner’s over, the kids have claimed the television and nobody’s ready to leave. Put a pot of McIntosh’s mulled Aperol on the stove for the spritz drinkers still on your sofa. Dry white wine, Aperol, apple cider and honey warm with orange and whole spices. It makes six servings and needs just 15 to 20 minutes over low heat. Don't let it boil. Ladle into mugs and let everyone settle in. The kitchen will smell like you had a plan.

#8263. Coach Mando's Advice For Dads Coaching Youth Sports

Brendan Wayne, the man who is The Mandalorian, has been coaching youth sports for more than 20 years. Here’s his advice to other coaches and parents on the sidelines.

When you watch the hit Star Wars TV show The Mandalorian — or the new film The Mandalorian and Grogu — and you start to wonder if there’s something about being a bounty hunter with a heart of gold that can help you with youth sports, you’re not nuts. It’s possible that just through osmosis, thanks to the motions of Mando himself, you’re getting some good sense of how to be a better sports parent. Here’s why: The actor who has played the body of The Mandalorian since 2019, Brendan Wayne, has been coaching soccer for 23 years. In addition to starting a new podcast, Hats & Helmets, Wayne is currently the coach of the Lady Lancers soccer team at Grant High School in California.

“I’ve played sports my whole life,” Wayne tells Fatherly. “It’s one of the greatest things a kid can learn to do.”

As the summer starts to give way to the beginning of school, we reached out to Wayne to get his core principles as a longtime coach of youth sports. This man may know how to calm down Baby Yoda, but that’s just acting. As a soccer coach, Wayne is an even bigger expert. Here’s his clear advice for parents of sporty kids, youth coaches, and why athletics can be great for all kinds of kids.

Wayne’s core coaching philosophy isn’t focused on winning; instead, he feels the only thing that makes a team is the notion of togetherness.

Many parents have been there. The game is going a certain way, and you can’t help yourself with your thoughts. You’ve shouted out something; you’ve even has words with a ref or the coach. What should you do? Wayne’s feelings are very, very clear.

Even as a coach, Wayne doesn’t shout at his players while the game is actually happening. The coaching comes before the game happens, not from the sidelines.

Sometimes, a kid can lose interest in their sport. Or maybe they’re feeling like they’re not part of the team. What can coaches and sports parents do? For Wayne, it’s not about quitting right away but about looking at athletics more holistically.

As an actor and performer, Wayne knows a thing or two about how to keep all aspects of his body in shape — fitting into that Mandalorian armor doesn’t just happen by accident. One of his biggest beliefs, which he applies to youth sports, is that a person has to look at the big picture. For Wayne, it’s all about making sure kids are getting different kinds of exercises.

If you do need to say something to a kid who looks frustrated out there in the game, keep in mind that most of these kids aren’t going pro. Some might, but that’s not the point of this moment.

When Wayne sees one of his kids on the field and they need inspiration, he sometimes just tries to lighten the moment.

#8262. Eight Sleep’s Alexandra Zatarain on women-centered tech, the science of better sleep, and planning a career around motherhood

By Sara Goldstein Updated Nov. 12, 2026

This article is sponsored by Eight Sleep. Thank you for supporting the brands that support Motherly and mamas.

Alexandra Zatarain helped build Eight Sleep into a tech unicorn, and she’s expecting her first child in January. Going through pregnancy while running a global company has reshaped how she sees her own body, her industry and the product she’s building. On this episode of The Motherly Podcast, the co-founder of the sleep-technology company talks about the research that showed Eight Sleep’s technology was improving men’s sleep more than women’s and what the company did about it, why sleep is the most important thing women can protect, and the career advice she wishes more women heard before becoming mothers.

Meet the expert: Alexandra Zatarain is the co-founder and VP of brand and marketing at Eight Sleep, the sleep-technology company behind the Pod. The Pod is an intelligent mattress cover that cools or heats each side to your ideal temperature automatically, maximizing deep sleep and minimizing wake-ups. A marketer and brand builder, she grew Eight Sleep from launch into a tech unicorn and helped create what the company calls the sleep fitness movement. Eight Sleep now sells in 37 countries. She’s expecting her first child in January with her husband, Matteo, the company’s co-founder and CEO.

Alexandra Zatarain: So many things. I just turned 37, and I’ve seen so many friends go through pregnancy before me. After my first trimester, I felt so bad, thinking, what a terrible friend I was. When you haven’t experienced it, you have such little empathy for what a woman’s body is going through, especially when life keeps demanding so much of you and it doesn’t stop. I really didn’t understand that you could feel so different in your body for so long. It’s built so much more admiration for women and what we go through, and it’s let me embrace a feminine side of myself that in tech you usually don’t get to bring out.

Alexandra Zatarain: It’s made me realize that the only way the world out there is going to change for our benefit as women and mothers is if more of us are the ones making the decisions. I just don’t see any way around it. We have a lot of parents at Eight Sleep, every executive on our team is a parent, but as a woman the experience is completely different. Unless we can share that first-hand knowledge, it’s going to be hard to make progress as fast as we need to. It’s unfortunate that it takes the first-person experience to become that advocate, because everyone should appreciate what mothers go through, given that we all come from a mother.

Alexandra Zatarain: A couple of years ago, our clinical team, which is more than 90% women, was analyzing data from our user base and noticed our technology had been improving men’s sleep more than women’s. They asked, what are we missing in how we design this? It turned out the algorithms that manage temperature while you sleep had been fed more data representing men than women. That’s a classic problem in science, where women are underrepresented because our bodies are more complex. You have to account for where someone is in their hormonal journey, pregnancy, postpartum, perimenopause. So we invested a couple million dollars into research and developed features from it. That changed how we think about ourselves, less about helping everyone in a broad way and more about solving specific problems women have had for ages.

Alexandra Zatarain: Sleep is the most important pillar of health. You would die sooner from sleep deprivation than from food deprivation, which tells you how fundamental it is. For women it matters even more because our hormones rule our lives, and sleep is the one tool we have to regulate them. If you sleep well, your chances of better hormonal balance go up significantly. It’s the best medicine we have, more than working out, more than any meal. The challenge is that those same hormones are often playing against us, making it harder to sleep well in different seasons of life, so keeping our routines as stable as possible helps counter what our bodies are going through.

Alexandra Zatarain: The mindset piece is really important. There’s so much going on, the anxiety, the intrusive thoughts, so not being too hard on yourself is the first step. Understanding that the season will pass should put you a little more at ease, because it’s not going to be your life forever. The other piece is setting yourself up with the right systems, and the most important one is available to everyone for free, which is routine. It helps your body a lot. When you do need to sleep, it’ll be easier for your body to fall asleep because it’s used to the schedule.

Alexandra Zatarain: I’m very rigid about my sleep schedule. I travel a lot, so sleep is number one for me. I make space for eight to nine hours every night, and I’m pretty good at hitting it. I go to bed by 9:30 or 10 every single night no matter where I am in the world, and I don’t really use an alarm unless I have to wake up before 6, because my body just wakes up on its own. That schedule is the thing that’s changed my life the most. Second to that is the environment, the temperature in my room and my bed, the lights going dark, no noise.

Alexandra Zatarain: I think of myself as an athlete, and we’re all sort of athletes in a way. My sport is making decisions about how to build this business, and that means I have to train, stay healthy and think long term. It’s not a sprint. We’ve been doing this for 12 years, so the question is how do I not burn out and stay here 20 or 30 years more. I’m also lucky I built this with my husband, so there’s no real line between business and personal life for us. It’s all mixed in, but it’s so purpose-driven that achieving that purpose every day is what feeds the energy.

Alexandra Zatarain: I’m very open with them about how intentional I was. I did my embryo freezing in my early 30s because of where I was in life. And I tell them that if they want a career after they have a family, the best time to build equity in that career is to push as hard as you can before. Know what you want, because time isn’t always on our side as women. Move up the ranks, so that by the time you have kids you have more flexibility and maybe a higher income. It is possible, but it takes planning, it will require compromises, and very importantly it will require the right partner.

Alexandra Zatarain: It starts with the people around you understanding what you truly need. Sometimes it’s as simple as the encouragement of, yes, go take a nap, yes, your body’s going through a lot. It gets harder once the baby’s home and the mom is maybe exclusively breastfeeding, because it really all falls on you. So have a plan in place ahead of time for how the load is going to be shared. Our partners are much more involved than previous generations, so have those conversations early. It doesn’t end with the birth plan. That’s where everything starts.

Alexandra Zatarain: The first trimester was difficult, a lot of nausea, and it was very hard to function at the level I’m used to. I almost never get sick, so feeling sick every day was a huge shift. It put me in the trajectory to build the team that would make it possible for me to become a mother, to figure out what to delegate and who to elevate, and I’ve built a stronger team as a result. But the biggest thing is that it’s taught me to let go. I can’t control how I feel every day. As a Type A person I always want to be in control, and this has been like therapy, learning that I’m not in control of my body. I’m building a human, and it’s fine if for this season things just work differently.

The school staff our kids love most are often the ones paid the least. Here’s how to thank them during American Education Week.

#8260. The Awkward Truth About Gym Class

Pretend you’re a tree. This was my earliest memory of physical education: our teacher, a tall and thin woman whose broad nimbus of dark hair was edged with gray, asking us to make-believe. By, as I understood it, not moving. In gym class. I was in second grade, and I was already confused. Somewhere here in my elementary school’s wood-floored gymnasium, I knew, there were ropes to climb, mats to tumble on, balls to kick and throw and dodge. And yet we were being corralled into this dumbed-down modern dance — the kind of hippie sh*t, I would later understand, that was typical of our Western Massachusetts college town.

Not that I was craving, or ever did crave, a traditional gym class. I was not made for gym. I was small — perpetually the second shortest boy in my grade — and slight and uninterested in the big sports that make up the bulk of public-school gym. I did not own a catcher’s mitt; no sane, responsible adult would let this shrimp play football.

At the same time, I was physical. I was a kid, after all. I wanted to run around, try a handstand, lift a dumbbell, shoot a basket, make a goal. And as uncoordinated and unenthusiastic as I was, I was not entirely untalented. I remember running a seven-minute mile in fourth grade. I could touch my toes and put one foot behind my head. My friend Jason and I competed to see who would be the first to knock out 60 sit-ups in a minute. I don’t remember who won.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class.

Those achievements and activities, however, had nothing to do with gym class as I experienced it. In the same way that English class was not designed to make philistines love literature, or biology to inspire dedication to the scientific method, gym class was not about converting us into athletes. Instead, it was a class for the kids who already were athletes, who played baseball and field hockey for fun, who owned weight machines at home, who didn’t need to sit through the gym teacher’s confounding explanation of what it meant to be “offsides.” I didn’t begrudge them their special class. I could spell and do algebra. They could throw an arcing spiral. This was the way of the world, even in a Massachusetts town full of ex-hippies.

And that all would have been just fine — if gym class had stuck with the most mainstream of sports. I could suck at soccer and blow at basketball, because who cared? Instead, gym class branched out, and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Swimming was a particular source of trauma. When I was 8, during a year my family spent living in Brighton, England, I was so tearfully reluctant to get in the pool that the headmaster of the school had to personally throw me in. And as I got older, the trauma morphed: Back in Massachusetts, the locker room after eighth-grade swimming lessons was a horror movie — I, the underdeveloped shrimp, had to undress surrounded by my Sasquatchian contemporaries. I have a memory of once changing entirely inside a locker, but that can’t be real. Those things were barely 10 inches wide. But another memory is definitely real: During one class, I dived into the deep end — and the force of the water as I entered yanked my swimsuit to my ankles. I don’t know how I had the wherewithal to pull them up before surfacing, but I did. I guess I was learning something.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class. Already awkward around girls, not to mention the implied romance of ballroom dance, I had the misfortune to be paired with Turtle Butt. Who was Turtle Butt? I don’t know. She was a girl I’d never spoken to, but one of my good friends had decided to call her Turtle Butt, even though, as far as I could tell, her butt did not resemble a turtle. And I was going to have to dance with her! Oh, the humiliation!

Gym class has always branched out from mainstream sports — and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Nearly 40 years later, I can now acknowledge that the humiliation was solely in my own head. I remember the potential embarrassment with infinitely more clarity than I remember any actual jeers or taunts, because there were none. But such is the world of the adolescent, where fears and anxieties dwarf reality.

And what I feared most of all was being seen. In other classes this didn’t happen. You might know where the Mason-Dixon Line was — or not. You might know how to deploy the quadratic formula — or not. Either way, you were not exposing anything about yourself other than your intellectual ability, or lack thereof.

It was similar in gym class. We all knew that some kids had it and some didn’t, and there was no shame in being terrible. (Asthma reduced my mile time to 20 minutes by eighth grade. But so what?) The difference, however, was that in gym class, unlike in history or math, you were a physical being. Strip away your ability to perform, and there you still stood, surrounded by your classmates, in sneakers and sweats or the jeans and T-shirt you wore to school that morning. You could pretend you’re a tree all you want — you remained visible: your prepubescent stature, your hairless lack of muscle tone, your terrapin posterior. There were no desks to hide behind, no escape from their eyes and their judgment.

No escape — except, perhaps, to grow up a little. In high school, my family moved to Southeastern Virginia, a place you’d think would have a sports and gym-class culture more extreme than that of the academic Yankees. Instead, gym was even more of an afterthought, not even required after sophomore or maybe junior year. Just like in second grade, I was confused. The school was full of jocks — guys who played soccer and football, girls on the field hockey team — and yet gym class was lackadaisical at best. Driver’s ed occupied a couple of months of the curriculum, and on Fridays, we’d ride a school bus to a nearby bowling alley, where nerds like me, who had no hope of throwing a strike, could at least show off by knowing how to score the game correctly.

Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not.

In fact, I considered the bowling alley my place — because I was there all the time, after school. Technically, not in the bowling alley, but just outside, where almost every day I would meet my skateboarder friends to ride the concrete drainage ditch next to its parking lot. In high school, skating had become my life, my all-consuming hobby, my… my… sport? Yes, my sport! After having failed at all of the mainstream sports, I’d finally found this one sweaty, filthy, wonderful way to be an athlete (though I would never have used that word back then). And while I wasn’t pro material, I wasn’t too bad at it, either. I could hold my own among my friends, at competitions in Virginia Beach, on road trips to Richmond and Washington, D.C. And more important, I could do so without fretting about being seen, in some unspeakable way, by the kids around me. Skateboarding required us to accept one another, in all our foibles and weirdnesses. Because if we didn’t, then who would we skate with?

I stuck with skateboarding for most of a decade, before aging out postcollege and taking up distance running and, more recently, rock climbing. As with skateboarding, I’m pretty good at both, if not truly exceptional, and I appreciate the physical experience of each in ways I could not have imagined in high school. At times, I’ve wondered: If gym class had taught us how to run, or how to scale a boulder, would I have discovered and loved those sports decades earlier? Somehow, I doubt it. Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not. What mattered was what happened after school, in every sense of the term. Still, gym class did teach me this one important lesson about public education: If you make like a tree, you can leave.

Some of this Amish farmer's gardening wisdom might sound old-fashioned, but his practical advice has plenty to teach modern gardeners.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Some of the best gardening tips never make it onto a seed packet. They come from people who've worked the same ground for years and notice what the rest of us walk past – like how a tomato leaf changes color before trouble starts.

I recently stumbled across a fascinating piece of gardening history that feels just as relevant today as it did when it was written. Back in 2013, Amish farmer Joni Miller sent Modern Farmer a 45-page handwritten essay on organic gardening and farming, packed with diagrams and advice on everything from compost to certification paperwork. All he asked in return was a two-year subscription.

Much of what Miller wrote will sound familiar to organic growers. Some of it surprised me, though, and it's fascinating to see how well his ideas line up with newer research. These are the eight lessons I found most interesting, and how to use each one at home.

Miller suggests making a little chart of leaf colors, and I love the idea of reading a vegetable bed that way. For tomatoes and eggplant, he says lower leaves that yellow once the plants start bearing give up their potassium to the fruit. A black, rotting spot on a tomato's bottom – aka blossom-end rot – in his experience, means poor calcium uptake.

Newer research largely agrees, though each symptom has other causes, too. Lower leaves also yellow from a nitrogen shortage, plain old age, or early blight (Alternaria linariae). Blossom-end rot does come from calcium not reaching the fruit, but the soil usually has plenty, and uneven watering tends to be the real trouble. I'd sort that out before buying fertilizer.

The weed section grabbed me most. Miller noticed foxtail and other grassy weeds sprouting better in tight, high-magnesium soils, and lambsquarters surging after heavy turkey manure. Velvetleaf liked rich ground, Canada thistle faded once soil was loose and cultivated, and pastures full of dandelions never grew lush. As he puts it, "Reading soils by their weeds is an art!"

Researchers read weeds the same way today, as clues with wiggle room. Weeds tolerate a range of conditions, so dandelions might mean compacted soil and chickweed might mean wet ground, or a neighbor's seed heads might just be blowing your way. Then confirm with a soil test, using a home kit that you send to a lab, like the MySoil Soil Test Kit, available on Amazon.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Miller's pest advice starts with life cycles, using squash bugs (Anasa tristis) as his example. The nymphs that hatch look like little spiders and start out soft. Each molt hardens them, and by the later ones, he found few organic sprays could touch them. If oil can't smother the eggs, his trick is to "target for those young spiderlings while they're easier prey."

That means turning squash leaves over. Look at the undersides, often in the crook between two veins, and you'll spot copper-brown egg clusters. Duct tape pulls them off easily. If a few nymphs get past you, insecticidal soap or neem oil, like Bonide Captain Jack's Neem Oil Spray, will knock them back, sprayed early or late, when bees are quieter. Adults, by then, are another story, and hand-picking works better on them.

Straw mulch is nothing new, so Miller's note about greenhouse tomato growers using alfalfa hay caught my attention. It keeps weeds down, but the bigger benefit, he says, is that "the decomposing alfalfa feeds the vegetables with high-quality nutrients."

Modern studies hold that up. Alfalfa is a legume, so it has more nitrogen than straw and breaks down faster. It holds moisture, too. Once the soil warms, spread 2–3 inches (5–8 cm) of weed-free hay around tomatoes and peppers, leaving a gap at the stems.

Ask if the hay field was sprayed, as some hay herbicides linger, and tomatoes are very sensitive. Can't find bales? Try using alfalfa meal instead, like Down to Earth organic alfalfa meal from Walmart.

I was surprised to learn you can time weeding with a thermometer. Miller counts heat units. You average each day's high and low, but a high over 90°F (32°C) only counts as 90, a low under 50°F (10°C) counts as 50, and you subtract 50. Weed seeds need about 60 units to germinate, he says, so he harrows right before that and starts back at zero with each new flush.

Weed researchers still study the same idea today, under the label stale seedbed, which is a funny name for it, honestly. Simply prepare the bed a few weeks early, water it, and wait for the first weeds, usually a week or two in warm soil. Slice them off in the top inch (2.5 cm) – digging deeper brings buried seeds up to sprout. WaLensee's stirrup-style action hoe from Home Depot suits that shallow work. Then sow without stirring the soil again.

This one sounded simple to me, and it is, just about. Miller waters his greenhouse plants in the forenoon, not the evening, and opens the vents on sunny days so plants don't stay damp. Fungal diseases, he warns, "explode in stale, damp environments."

Current advice backs him up. Picture tomatoes watered at dusk, still wet at midnight. That's where early blight and gray mold (Botrytis cinerea) get going. Water the soil in the morning instead, space and stake plants for airflow, and stay out of wet rows. Greenhouses need open vents or a fan, and patio pots need elbow room.

For run-down soil, Miller says green manure crops really help, along with soil tests. Bare soil takes a beating from winter rain. A cover crop holds it with roots and shades out weeds, too. Turned in or left on top, it adds organic matter. Legumes like crimson clover and field peas also pull nitrogen from the air, with help from root bacteria.

This late in fall, I'd go with cereal rye. Oats and field peas want a late-summer start, and a cold winter usually finishes them off. Crimson clover, available from Outsidepride on Amazon, needs a few weeks of growth before hard frost – unless your winters are mild, that one's an early-fall job. In spring, cut the crop around flowering, before seed sets, then wait two to three weeks to plant.

Farmers in Miller's community save back their own soybean seed, which he says "helps that variety to somewhat adapt to your farm's soil type." You don't need a farm for it. Save seed from several of your healthiest, most productive open-pollinated plants, not one favorite, and do it again the year after, too. Little by little, your seed comes from plants that thrive in your garden.

Beans, peas, lettuce, and tomatoes are the easy ones, because their flowers mostly pollinate themselves. Squash, cucumbers, and corn need isolation or hand-pollination, since bees and wind can cross them with nearby varieties. I'd skip F1 hybrids, though, since their seed can come up quite different. Dry your seeds well, then store them somewhere cool in labeled kraft paper seed envelopes.

Much of Miller's letter covers certification forms, buffer strips, and ice houses. But tucked in between are gardening ideas that today's research still backs up. Next season, I'm taking a slower look at my weeds and tomato leaves. You might notice things you've been walking past for years.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#8256. 10 Great Sports Docs & True-Life Stories To Stream With Your Kids Right Now

From inspiring stories to crucial moments in history to cutting edge contermporary atheletes, there’s a great co-viewing experience for everyone.

Finding movies and TV that please everyone can be tough. But if you’ve got a sporty kid, screen time is a great opportunity. Sure, there’s old-school sports movie like The Sandlot or A League of Their Own — complete with inspirational messages and strong moral codes. But why go for fictional sports stories when you can get the real thing?

Sports docuseries, or true-to-life dramatized sports stories, are great to watch with young athletes. They tell inspirational tales and maybe even give them a real-life role model in the meantime. From a variety of different sports to a selection of different formats, we’ve thought about the watchability and the relevance of each of these selections. There should be something for everyone in this list. And, at the very least, with each, you and your kid will learn something.

This documentary film focuses on several different Paralympic athletes, all of whom have truly amazing stories. Warning for parents: This documentary is not for the faint of heart, as some of the physical challenges are truly harrowing. For example, Bebe Vio — who inspired the name of the documentary — lost all of her limbs to meningitis at the age of 11. She nonetheless went on to become a wheelchair fencer. Deeply inspiring, this doc is great for teens interested in sports and perhaps great for all of us to have a little perspective on the amazing nature of the human spirit.

The 2004 story of the Boston Red Sox is a great one in terms of an underdog story. Even if you’re not a Red Sox fan, this story represents a very specific time in baseball and tells the story of how this iconic team broke a curse that had existed since 1918. If your kid is just starting to get into baseball, this documentary series might seem like ancient history; after all, 2004 was more than 20 years ago. And yet, this particular season for many of us feels very recent and still relevant.

Who doesn’t love trick shots? This 30 for 30 ESPN doc is all about a group of five guys who were former college roommates who created a sports comedy entertainment phenomenon. Focused on trick shots and betting, this doc is 100% for older kids. But if you’ve got a teen who is into sports and loves to joke around, this is a great, quirky documentary focused on male friendship, humor, and creating something nobody has ever done before.

Everybody is obsessed with Travis Kelce, but his brother Jason Kelce might be the more interesting of the siblings, at least as an athlete. The 2023 documentary film chronicles the 2022 Philadelphia Eagles season, with a specific focus on Kelce. The main tension here is whether or not Kelce will retire from the NFL. Weird topic for kids? Well, for tweens and teens interested in unpacking the real-deal toll of being in the NFL, there’s something smartly educational about this. You may be young and obsessed with football now, but life is long.

Not technically a documentary, this is a docudrama based on the true story of Ray McElrathbey, who deals with a ton of family adversity and racism. Set in the early 2000s, McElrathbey’s story is inspiring and very family-oriented. Again, this one might be for older kids, but the script is from Nick Santora of Reacher and Sopranos fame, so there’s a breezy and very focused feeling to this movie.

Here’s another docudrama that is based on a real-life movement in India, centered on teenagers and skateboarding culture. In the film, a young girl named Prerna (Rachel Sanchita Gupta) finds purpose and belonging through skateboarding. The film is a heartwarming coming-of-age movie, but watching it with your kid means you’re also giving them a dose of contemporary history. The production for the film also worked very closely with rural villages in India to make sure it accurately portrayed the culture and struggles of teenagers.

A great one to watch with your aspiring skateboarding kid, or maybe a kid who isn’t sure what their athletic interest might be.

One of the greatest athletes of our time is also the subject of a one-of-a-kind docuseries. Released in 2024, Simone Biles Rising is all about the gymnast’s comeback. The fact that Biles has been so transparent about her mental health has been a groundbreaking part of the conversations about young athletes. As both a role model and someone who is part of living history, Biles is a figure that should inspire conversation with your curious athlete.

This 10-part documentary changed everything back in 2020. However, at this point, The Last Dance — which tells the story of one of the greatest periods of the Chicago Bulls — almost feels vintage. Chances are, for certain parents, you didn’t have a kid old enough to watch this documentary nearly seven years ago. And, if you’re of the generation that lived through the Bulls’ 1990s dynasty, then you owe it to share that history with your kid.

Not everything about Michael Jordan and his teammates is admirable, to be clear. But the thing about some great sports history is that it can be messy.

Focused on the 2024 X Games, The Rise: Gold Medal Girls of the X Games focuses on four teen athletes, Arisa Trew, Shiloh Catori, Reese Nelson, and Jada Ward. Those are all skateboarders, and that’s just the most recent season. More broadly, The Rise covers all sorts of women’s sports, from skating to the WNBA. If you have a young woman looking for some new role models, you can’t miss with the various seasons of The Rise.

You can really start anywhere with this excellent docuseries. But the most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained is focused on the 2024 Tour de France. Obviously, the famous bicycle race has existed since 1903, but it’s really only recently that we could actually document this incredible event. Even the least sporty kid in the world can get excited about people using their bodies to propel a bicycle forward. And the most sporty kids will have trouble wrapping their mind around the sheer effort it takes to traverse 2,200 miles over 24 days over some of the hilliest terrain on Earth.

The most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained, released in 2025, is now the last season of this docuseries. The real Tour de France hasn’t gone anywhere, of course. In fact, it’s happening right now. Meaning if you get your kid excited enough, you can watch the 2026 Tour de France as it’s happening. Or watch a little contemporary Tour de France, then go back and watch Unchained on Netflix.

#8255. Ten Deaths & 5,400 Cases Later, The U.S. Has Lost Its Measles Elimination Status

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a subgroup of the World Health Organization, will make the official announcement today.

Measles has made headlines time and time again over the past two years, as cases have hit record highs and vaccination rates have reached record lows. Now, the looming threat has come true: according to sources familiar with the vote, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) revoked the United States’ measles elimination status.

The group is expected to make a formal announcement today.

To date, the U.S. has racked up more than 5,400 confirmed measles cases in 2026, the most to be reported in the United States in 35 years. There have been 10 reported measles-related deaths so far, including an infant in Wisconsin earlier this month. Measles was considered officially eliminated in the U.S. in 2000, meaning there had been no large outbreaks or uncontrolled domestic transmission of the virus for at least 12 months prior.

America’s current measles outbreaks first began in January 2025 in West Texas. By January 2026, the spread continued unchecked. PAHO’s meeting to discuss the country’s measles elimination status was originally scheduled for April 2026, KFF reports, but the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) asked for more time to determine whether measles cases were being transmitted domestically or “imported” (for example, if someone contracted measles abroad and then brought it to the U.S.). According to NBC, measles is now considered endemic to the U.S.

Many issues have contributed to the country’s ongoing measles outbreaks, from sweeping funding and staffing cuts to public health agencies to a lack of leadership — there was no Senate-confirmed director of the CDC for an entire year during this measles outbreak. But the main driver is declining vaccination rates, which experts blame on the Trump administration, specifically HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr, as Scary Mommy previously reported.

The CDC and American Academy of Pediatrics both recommend children get their first measles vaccine dose between 12 and 15 months of age, and the second dose between 4 and 6 years of age before starting school. According to CDC data, 96% of measles cases in 2026 have occurred in unvaccinated individuals. A KFF poll found that roughly one in five adults believe getting the measles vaccine is more dangerous than becoming infected with the measles. Parents are commonly exposed to vaccine misinformation, and data shows it is affecting their health decisions: the number of kindergarteners with vaccine exemptions rose to 4.2% in the 2025-2026 school year, the highest in the country’s history, with 39 states falling below the 95% vaccinated threshold needed to prevent outbreaks.

“The expected loss of America’s status as having eradicated measles will be a tragedy because it reflects the preventable loss of human lives. It is unthinkable that people in the United States should be dying from measles in 2026,” said Wendy S. Armstrong, M.D., president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America, in a publicly issued statement. “Our government’s leaders and public health officials must heed this urgent warning and take actions that slow the spread. That starts with promoting vaccination against measles, which is proven to be safe and effective.”

The largest outbreak in the U.S. since it earned measles elimination status, prior to the current one, was in 2018-2019. It was curtailed through a strong federal and state-level public health response, including closing schools where transmission occurred, prohibiting unvaccinated children from attending school, and fining parents for not vaccinating their children, KFF reports. The CDC also declared a public health emergency and made “clear statements about the importance of measles vaccinations.”

But last week, CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz told Reuters that the agency will not make any major changes to their handling of the outbreak regardless of PAHO’s decision. The CDC will continue to “help [the states] provide awareness about ​measles, emphasizing, reemphasizing that the number one way to prevent measles is the MMR (combined measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine,” she said.

She attributed the ongoing spread of measles to “closely knit communities” — several outbreaks have started in religious communities, like among the Pennsylvania Amish, where vaccination rates are lower than other parts of the country.

“These communities typically don’t vaccinate their children...their families were making decisions about the MMR vaccine 20 to 30 years ago and we’re just now seeing the results of those decisions,” Schwartz said.

In response, the AAP and nearly 150 other health care organizations published a letter calling on Kennedy Jr. and Schwartz to develop and implement a plan to eliminate measles in the United States. Their recommendations include restoring evidence-based immunization policies, proactively encouraging measles vaccination, and conveying accurate information about measles and MMR vaccines.

This article was originally published on November 9, 2026

#8254. Your kid needs you to have hobbies outside of motherhood. Here’s why

Hobbies aren’t a luxury for moms. They boost well-being, nurture identity, and show our children what a full life looks like.

By Lauren Ramakrishna Updated Nov. 13, 2026

Twenty-four years. That’s how long it had been since I last stood atop a swim block, preparing to dive in for a timed race in an official meet.

A whistle blew. The crowd hushed to silence. A monotone call came over the loudspeaker, “Swimmers, take your mark,” followed by a loud electronic beep that signaled the start of the race. I felt the cold rush of water overtake my body upon diving in. The neurons in my brain feverishly told my muscles to complete the strokes I’d learned decades before. In seconds, it was done. I finished the race.

When I got out of the pool, I walked over to my kids. My son, a competitive swimmer himself, looked at me and earnestly said, “Wow, Mom. I’m proud of you.”

Like most moms, I have a packed schedule. I work, parent, volunteer at school, shepherd my two kids to practices and social gatherings, throw meals together, walk the dog, and occasionally find a moment to breathe. But over the past couple of years, I watched my growing kids, now ages 12 and 9, discover and engage in passions that light them up. It left me wondering, why not me, too?

“A recurring theme in my practice is women feeling they’ve lost their individual identities somewhere between work, parenting, and meeting everyone else’s needs,” says Carly Snyder, a New York City–based reproductive and perinatal psychiatrist. “Part of my work involves helping women recognize that their own interests and needs are legitimate.”

In an effort to start prioritizing my own interests, I jumped at the chance to sign up for a summer swim league for adults aptly named “Grown-Up Swimming.” The whole experience reignited my love for swimming, and it showed me and my kids that I’m more than just a mom.

Research highlights a multitude of benefits earned by pursuing hobbies. Hobbyists often have wider social networks, improved mental health markers, and enhanced positive emotions.

Hobbies offer a particularly important lifeline for mothers, who often report losing themselves to the demanding needs of family life. That rings true for Kaitlyn Edington, an art educator and mom of two who recalls struggling after returning to work as a teacher following the birth of her first child. “I was so depleted,” Edington says. She spent her workdays teaching with short breaks to pump, often bringing her computer into her pumping room so she could catch up on work, then went home to full nights of infant care.

One day while scrolling on Instagram, Edington saw an artist posting images of her sketchbook paintings. “She changed my life,” Edington says. “Her sketchbook paintings were so loose and free, and she was encouraging people to draw everyday. I remember thinking, ‘If I have to pump two to three times a day, which I absolutely hate, why not pair it with something that I love?’” From then on, Edington sketched when she pumped, and ultimately developed a habit of daily sketching that she continues 10 years later.

No longer in the pumping phase of life, Edington ensures she gets time to sketch by waking up before her kids. “I hold the habit of waking up before my kids as sacred,” she says. “I need that time, when nobody needs me. It’s my emotional rest.”

Science backs Edington’s belief that her hobby stabilizes her mental health. “Reengaging in meaningful, enjoyable activities can be therapeutically valuable,” Snyder says. “Behavioral activation, an evidence-based treatment for depression, specifically emphasizes reconnecting with activities that provide pleasure, purpose, or a sense of accomplishment.”

Snyder has three children, ages 19, 16, and 11, and throughout their lives she has maintained her dedication to skiing, cycling, yoga and running, completing a total of 19 marathons. She knows her kids benefit from her hobbies. Each time Snyder trains for an upcoming marathon, “[My kids] witness my commitment, discipline, setbacks, and perseverance,” she says. “Watching a parent pursue a hobby provides opportunities to observe persistence, emotional regulation, problem-solving, and enjoyment.”

But those benefits are secondary to the impacts hobbies have on the women pursuing them. “I think we’ve become so accustomed to framing everything mothers do in terms of how it benefits their children,” Snyder says. “Women are entitled to happiness and fulfillment for their own sake.”

It’s simply an added bonus that when mom is happy for mom’s sake, the benefits for her kids naturally follow, according to multiple studies linking a mother’s well-being with her child’s. Plus, kids also learn that all stages of adulthood, including those under the umbrella of parenting, can include personal fulfillment, curiosity, and growth.

The best way to start a hobby is to let yourself reconnect with something you already love. I remembered how much joy I got out of competing in swim meets in high school, and I was eager to recreate that glee. Ask yourself, “What did I love when I was a kid or a young adult?”

Your hobby doesn’t have to involve intense commitment. “Reading, gardening, dancing, listening to music, or simply spending time alone can be just as meaningful as running a marathon,” Snyder says.

Search online for local groups involved in the activity you want to pursue. Your local library may have resources to help you get started as well.

When you’re ready to commit, set realistic goals. Start by focusing on your hobby consistently for just 10-15 minutes per day. Showing up is the main goal.

“Motherhood should expand a woman’s identity, not erase it,” Snyder advises. Which hobby will help expand yours?
