#8216. The Silent Health Problem Vets Say Most Cat Owners Never See Coming

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Dental disease is one of the most common health problems seen by vets, yet it's also one of the easiest to overlook. Cats are particularly good at hiding discomfort, so a cat with painful teeth or inflamed gums may carry on behaving normally for a surprisingly long time.

By the time obvious signs appear, the problem may already have been developing for months or even longer, and suddenly a minor issue is a major disaster. The good news is that dental disease is largely preventable, and keeping a cat's teeth healthy doesn't necessarily mean relying on a toothbrush alone.

Plaque is where the problem begins. It forms when bacteria mix with saliva and food particles on the surface of the teeth. If plaque isn't removed, it can harden into tartar â aka calculus â within days.

Tartar leads to inflammation of the gums, a condition known as gingivitis. This can progress to periodontitis, an infection involving the tooth root, weakening the attachment between the gum and the tooth, and eroding enamel. Eventually, the tooth starts breaking down from the inside.

These conditions can all be painful. A cat with advanced dental disease may drool, paw at its mouth, drop food while eating, or stop eating altogether. Bad breath, bloody saliva, teeth chattering, and even sneezing can also be warning signs.

Unfortunately, cats don't always make their discomfort obvious, which is why prevention is so important.

Regular toothbrushing remains the most effective way to prevent dental disease in cats. Daily brushing removes plaque before it has the chance to harden into tartar and tackles one of the main causes of dental problems.

A toothbrush or finger brush designed for cats should be used with toothpaste specifically formulated for felines. Human toothpaste contains ingredients that can be harmful if swallowed.

It's much easier to establish the habit when a cat is young, making it an enjoyable, even fun part of their routine. Older cats can learn too, although a slow approach with plenty of positive reinforcement gives the best chance of success.

Even brushing every few days is better than not brushing at all, although daily brushing provides the greatest benefit.

For cats that arenât tolerating a brush, dental wipes can be a good option.

For cats that won't tolerate brushing, dental diets and treats can provide another option. Dental dry foods contain ingredients and have a texture that are designed to help reduce plaque formation. The limitation is that not every cat actually chews its food. Some cats swallow their food with very little chewing, which reduces the potential benefit.

When choosing dental products, the Veterinary Oral Health Council seal is a useful indicator of effectiveness. Products carrying the VOHC seal have been independently tested and shown to reduce plaque or tartar.

Prescription dental diets are also available through veterinarians. They typically use oversized kibble designed to encourage more contact with the teeth during chewing and may be worth considering for cats with a history of dental problems.

Dental treats and chews have a similar action to dental diets, but are often made from more palatable ingredients to encourage cats to chew them. As a result, they can be quite high in calories, so make sure you include them in your catâs daily allowance.

More recently, powders containing brown algae or seaweed have been showing promising results in the fight against tartar formation, but some cats arenât keen on the taste.

Oral rinses offer another preventative option for cats that resist brushing and aren't suitable for dietary changes. They can be applied using gauze or a soft cloth and work by chemically reducing plaque and tartar before they build up.

The VOHC seal can again help when choosing between products. A veterinarian can also recommend an appropriate rinse for an individual cat.

Water additives are one of the easiest dental care options because they are simply added to a cat's drinking water. They work by helping inhibit plaque formation.

There are some important limitations, however. A cat that doesn't drink enough water may not receive much benefit, while some additives can change the smell or taste of the water enough that a cat avoids drinking it.

A VOHC-approved water additive can be a useful addition to a broader dental care routine, but it is unlikely to be enough on its own.

Plaque prevention gels are often used after a professional dental cleaning. They can help protect newly cleaned teeth and extend the time before another cleaning is needed.

Veterinarians commonly recommend these gels as a follow-up to professional dental treatment rather than as a standalone daily solution. Any instructions about feeding and drinking after application should be followed carefully.

Even cats receiving regular dental care at home may eventually need a professional cleaning. This is performed under general anesthesia, allowing the veterinarian to clean below the gum line, examine each tooth closely, take dental X-rays when necessary, and identify teeth that need to be removed.

The need for anesthesia can understandably concern some owners, but untreated dental disease can lead to chronic pain, infection, and systemic illness.

Senior cats and cats with a history of dental problems may also need their teeth assessed more frequently than during a standard annual examination. Finding problems early generally means treatment can be simpler and less invasive.

There has been a rise in the number of businesses offering dentals without anesthesia, at a price much lower than a dental procedure with your vet. While the idea of a cheaper dental cleaning without the worry of your cat going under anesthetic is appealing, the most significant periodontal disease happens below the gumline. Cats in particular are susceptible to a painful condition known as feline oral resorptive lesions (FORLs), in which the tooth slowly dissolves. FORLs can develop in completely clean teeth. They often form in the roots and need to be diagnosed using dental x-ray.

A catâs teeth may look clean after an anesthetic-free dental, but there could be painful problems going on beneath the surface.

Dental disease isn't inevitable, but preventing it requires more than waiting for obvious symptoms to appear. Cats can hide dental pain remarkably well, meaning a seemingly healthy mouth may already have problems developing beneath the surface.

Regular brushing is the most effective option, but dental diets, treats, rinses, water additives, and professional cleaning can all play a role. The right combination will depend on the individual cat and how well they tolerate each approach.

Keeping on top of dental care can help prevent painful problems from becoming something a cat has to quietly live with for years.

Christmas cacti are incredibly fussy about their environment so if you want a fabulous display of festive flowers, avoid these blooming disaster zones.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For a plant that’s such an iconic part of our festive decorations, the Christmas cactus is surprisingly sensitive when it comes to flowering well. Put this beloved houseplant in the wrong spot in your home and its flowerbuds could even drop off – yes, every last precious one! So, it pays to know what conditions will keep your Christmas cactus happy, and the common spots that will likely lead to a dramatic bud drop and zero holiday blooms.

When we think of cacti, most of us naturally picture a dry desert environment baking under a scorching sun. But Christmas cacti evolved to live in the rainforests of Brazil, where they thrive in damp air and dappled sunlight. They don’t grow in soil in the ground but cling to tree branches or shady rock crevices, their roots anchored in small pockets of decomposing leaves. And that’s a far cry from living in a pot of soil in the dry air of our well-heated homes – which is why Shlumbergera can be so persnickety about the conditions they require to flower well.

Once you appreciate why your plant is so fussy, it’s easy to give a Christmas cactus everything it needs in November and December to swell its buds into bounteous blooms. And if you’ve gone to the effort of persuading a Christmas cactus to bloom right on time for the holidays, don't waste all your hard work by putting your plant in the wrong spot now! For a glorious cascade of flowering stems to add to your holiday decor, these are the five spots to avoid.

Developing buds and blooms require a tremendous amount of energy, and a Christmas cactus gets 100% of this from sunlight. While Shlumbergera needs regular periods of dark to set its buds, as soon as you spot those tiny dots of color on the stem ends, the plant needs to be moved to get more light, otherwise it won’t have enough energy to develop them into flowers.

The type of light is important, too. Because Christmas cacti naturally live in a rainforest under a canopy of leaves, indirect sunlight is best. That simply means putting your plant in a bright, sunny room but in a spot where it’s not directly hit by sunlight. East- and west-facing rooms are typically best for high levels of indirect light to get a Christmas cactus to flower well.

If there’s not enough natural light in the spot you’d like your plant to be, then a basic dimmable LED grow light such as this from Walmart is the easy answer.

We know that adequate light is vital if a Christmas cactus is to flower, and in the rainforest beneath a dense tree canopy, sunshine is a precious commodity. So Shlumbergera buds lock onto the direction light is coming from – and if you then move the plant, buds will twist towards the changed light source. This sudden environmental shift stresses the plant and buds will likely drop off.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

This phototropism only begins once the flowerbuds start to form a teardrop shape or reach around ¼ inch long, so you have until then to decide exactly where to position your plant for the holidays. Even the slightest rotation causes the plant to waste energy on reorienting buds to the light source, so to get the best possible flower display, many folk draw a small pencil line on the pot and the surface it’s sitting on, so it’s easy to realign if it does get knocked. If you’re using a grow light, mark its position, too, and be careful not to move it.

Once they’ve set their buds, Christmas cacti like a fairly even temperature of around 65-70°F, which happily is the cozy range most of us keep our homes heated to. In their native rainforest where temperatures are normally highly stable, a blast of cold air may herald a life-threatening freeze so can trigger the cactus to immediately enter survival mode. And it's pretty dramatic: if temperatures suddenly dip, Shlumbergera can react by ditching its buds or flowers to conserve energy so it can concentrate on keeping its core alive. This natural response happens just the same in a draft of cold air from a window or when an exterior door is opened and closed.

Ripening fruit produces a harmless gas, ethylene. All fruit that can still ripen after picking – apples, pears, peaches, tomatoes and avocados as well as bananas – produce ethylene, and that’s the exact same gas a Christmas cactus emits when it’s stressed enough to enter survival mode. Understandable, then, that Shlumbergera are incredibly sensitive to this gas, and simply sitting next to a fruit bowl can be enough to trigger Christmas cactus bud drop.

As this plant naturally evolved to grow in a humid environment, Christmas cacti can really struggle in the dry, heated air of our homes to start with. But place the plant anywhere near a heating vent, radiator or fireplace where the air is continually stripped of moisture, and stems will quickly dehydrate and buds brown, dropping off before the flowers even open. This is one of the most common reasons for a Christmas cactus not flowering as these houseplants are often put on a fireplace mantelpiece or windowsill above a radiator over the holidays.

So, positioning your Shlumbergera well away from any heat source is a must. Take the next step and give your plant the humidity it craves, however, and it will not only flower more profusely but those hydrated blooms will last for longer. Thanks to the regular steam from showers, cooking and kettles, bathrooms and kitchens typically have air that’s moist enough for a Christmas cactus to thrive and, in other rooms, a humidity tray is the solution.

Standing a Christmas cactus on a Bonsai pebble tray such as this from Lowe’s is ideal, or make your own with a plant saucer and pea gravel pebbles like this Landscape Rock from The Home Depot. The plant must sit on the pebbles above the water level so, rather than being drawn up into the potting soil, the water evaporates to add moisture to the air. Another simple way to increase air humidity is to group your Christmas cactus with other houseplants as they’ll form their own microclimate.

If you've been wondering where to put a Christmas cactus, now you know the common places to rule out. It's well worth searching out just the right spot as when a Christmas cactus gets the sunlight, stability and humidity it needs as fall deepens into winter, you’ll be surprised how much more enthusiastically it flowers. Happy holidays!

Throughout October, we are throwing our support behind the mission to turn Feral Cat Day into Feral Cat Awareness Month, an opportunity to raise awareness about community cats (also called feral or stray), promote Trap-Neuter-Return, and recognize the millions of caring people who dedicate their time and energy to improving the lives of the cats & kittens most in need of support. With around 60-100 million stray cats in the US, we know it takes more than just one day to make a meaningful difference in a problem this overwhelming, and one group that understands this more than most is The Cat Network in Miami, Florida.

Founded in 1995, The Cat Network is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization supported by more than 2,500 volunteers and donors, helping community cats, stray, abandoned, and homeless cats throughout South Florida while supporting the people who care for them. Through education, low-cost spay/neuter services, adoption assistance, and advocacy, the organization works to humanely reduce cat overpopulation and improve the lives of cats and the communities they live in.

The Cat Network is dedicated to humanely reducing cat overpopulation in South Florida through five core pillars: education, sterilization, adoption, advocacy, and humane public policy. Our story begins more than 30 years agoâ¦

In July 1995, the City Manager of Miami Beach contracted with a commercial trapper, Humane Animal Removal, to trap and euthanize the cityâs feral cats, with a bounty of $35.00 for each cat trapped and killed. When this became public, a local and national outcry ensued, and the media had a field day. The Cat Network, still in its infancy, helped organize local opposition to the trap-kill plan. Susan Fleming, president of The Cat Network and a Miami Beach resident, was instrumental in negotiating with the City to institute TNR instead.  With help from Animal Controlâs mobile animal clinic and SoBe spay/neuter certificates, we convinced the City to implement the more humane approach of TNR.

The following year, we began our spay/neuter certificate program with participating veterinary clinics, the first of which was Galloway Animal Clinic. Since 1995, we've helped sterilize more than 122,000 cats and assisted in the adoption of more than 24,000 cats.

What makes us unique is our comprehensive approach. Rather than simply responding to the symptoms of overpopulation, we focus on preventing future litters while helping cats in need. Our programs include the Miami Meow Mobile, low-cost spay/neuter vouchers, adoption referrals through an extensive foster network, public education, and advocacy for Trap-Neuter-Return (TNR) as the most humane and effective way to manage community cat populations.

One of our biggest challenges is simply the sheer number of cats needing help. Because South Florida has warm weather year-round, kitten season never truly ends. This creates an ongoing demand for spay and neuter services, foster homes, adoptions, and community education. Every day we receive calls from residents who have discovered kittens, injured cats, or growing community cat colonies.

There really isn't an "off season" for cat rescue here, so our volunteers and veterinary programs stay busy throughout the entire year. Preventing unwanted litters through early sterilization is one of the most effective ways to reduce this constant cycle.

Funding is another ongoing challenge. Keeping our veterinary programs affordable requires significant community support, and the costs of medical supplies, equipment, and operations continue to rise.

People can make an enormous difference by:

Becoming a volunteer or foster caregiver.

Sharing our educational resources and adoptable cats on social media.

Every donation, volunteer hour, and shared post helps save lives.

Over the past 30 years, The Cat Network has become one of South Florida's leading organizations dedicated to reducing cat overpopulation. Sterilizing more than 122,000 cats and helping over 24,000 cats find homes are milestones that represent countless lives saved.

We're especially proud of the Miami Meow Mobile, which has dramatically increased access to affordable veterinary care, and our long-standing network of volunteers and foster caregivers who make our adoption program possible. Together, these programs have helped thousands of residents become part of the solution while improving animal welfare throughout South Florida.

The Miami Meow Mobile is a fully equipped veterinary clinic designed specifically for cats. Originally envisioned in 2001 and launched in 2005, it was created to make affordable veterinary care accessible to more people throughout the community.

Today, the Meow Mobile provides low-cost spay and neuter surgeries, vaccinations, testing, microchipping, parasite treatments, and basic wellness services. Originally designed as a traveling clinic, it currently operates from a fixed location in Kendall, allowing us to serve a large number of cats efficiently and safely.

The Meow Mobile remains one of our signature programs because every surgery performed helps prevent future litters and reduces shelter overcrowding throughout South Florida.

Our Spay/Neuter Certificate Program partners with participating veterinarians throughout South Florida. Residents can purchase discounted certificates that cover sterilization surgery, a rabies vaccination, and ear tipping for community cats.

This partnership expands access to affordable veterinary care beyond our own clinic. If someone discovers a stray or community cat in their neighborhood, the voucher program provides an affordable pathway to have that cat sterilized before additional litters are born.

By working together with local veterinary clinics, we're able to reach far more cats than we could alone and give residents practical tools to help solve the community cat problem.

Working with cats means no two days are ever alike. Volunteers have rescued kittens from engine compartments, construction sites, shopping centers, and backyard sheds. Every rescue brings its own surprisesâand often a few scratches and plenty of memorable stories.

The resilience of these cats never stops amazing us. Watching frightened community kittens transform into affectionate family pets is one of the most rewarding experiences we witness over and over again.

Every cat that is sterilized prevents countless future kittens from being born into homelessness. Every adoption changes two livesâthe cat's and the family's.

Knowing that thousands of volunteers, donors, veterinarians, and community members are working together toward the same goal makes every success even more meaningful.

As we celebrate over 30 years of service, our goal remains the same: continuing to expand access to affordable spay and neuter serviceswhile working toward a future where no healthy or treatable cat is euthanized simply because there are too many homeless animals.

We continue to strengthen our community partnerships, grow volunteer involvement, support foster caregivers, and educate the public about responsible pet ownership and Trap-Neuter-Return practices.

Anyone interested in getting involved can learn more by visiting TheCatNetwork.org. There they can become a member, volunteer, foster cats, adopt, donate, or schedule services through the Miami Meow Mobile.

#8212. Chatting About Safe Scruffing Education, Feline Altruism, and Our Guest, Cyril | Chatty Cattys, Episode 38

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

In this episode of Catsterâs Chatty Cattys podcast, Dr. Karyn and Nicole tackle the controversial topic of scruffing, while also sharing some fun comparisons between cats, dogs, and toddlers. Instead of treating scruffing like an absolute taboo, the hosts break down why understanding a cat's specific boundaries can make quick vet visits or home care way less stressful for everyone. Dr. Karyn brings her cat, Sirill, onto the desk to show why a timid pinch fails, how a solid hold gives cats a sense of security, and how to quickly test if your cat is way too sensitive for the technique.

Get the real scoop on scruffing catsâincluding why total bans ignore harm reduction when you just need to safely pull out a thorn or trim nails in a pinch. Dr. Karyn breaks down the biggest mistakes pet parents make, explaining why delicately pinching a bit of skin only annoys your cat and how a full-hand hold actually provides better control and stability. Youâll also learn how to check your catâs tolerance before even trying a hold so you never accidentally upset a sensitive pet.

Plus, the hosts chat about research comparing how dogs, cats, and toddlers help others, debating whether cats are truly selfish or just super selective about their time. From winning over shy rescue cats to comparing dogs to needy toddlers and cats to moody teenagers, this episode offers a relaxed, relatable look at living with felines.

Rethinking the Scruffing Debate: Dr. Karyn and Nicole discuss how complete anti-scruffing rules miss the mark on practical care. They explain that learning safe restraint acts as harm reduction, letting you handle fast tasks like pulling out a thorn or trimming claws without having to resort to full sedation.

Test Sensitivity First: Before going in for a hold, Dr. Karyn recommends checking the neck area with gentle pets and tickles. If a cat flinches or pulls away (like her cat, Zelda), you should never try to scruff them.

Skip the "Pinch": The most common mistake people make is grabbing a tiny pinch of skin, which just annoys the cat and provokes a fight. Proper restraint needs a full, firm hand on the scruff so the cat feels secure and can't wriggle free.

Never Pick Them Up by the Scruff: The hosts emphasize that while a hand on the scruff helps keep a cat grounded, you should never lift or carry an adult cat this way.

Altruism in Pets vs. Toddlers: The conversation turns to research comparing toddlers, dogs, and cats. Studies show dogs and kids will help out even without a reward, while cats generally step in only when thereâs something clear in it for them.

Earned Love Feels Extra Special: Nicole and Dr. Karyn talk about how dogs offer constant, people-pleasing affection, whereas a catâs love feels like an earned privilege. That conditional nature is exactly what makes it so rewarding when a quiet cat finally comes over to snuggle.

As a certified cat-lover, Radim was excited to join the Catster team on the mission to help all the cat parents in the world by providing useful and helpful information. He used to live with two wonderful cats before embarking on his travels around the world. Radim currently lives in Slovakia, surrounded by nature and his neighbors' cat community.

#8211. What’s That Smell??? How To Tell the Difference Between Normal Stinky Dog Breath and A Warning Sign

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

A dog's breath is never going to be minty fresh, but there's a big difference between ordinary doggy breath and an odor that's genuinely foul. A healthy dog's mouth should have a mild smell, often with a faint trace of whatever they last ate. When that smell suddenly becomes fishy, rotten, or unusually unpleasant, it can be a sign that something else is going on.

Bad breath can have several possible causes, ranging from common dental problems to health conditions that need urgent veterinary attention. Knowing what that smell might be telling you can make it easier to recognize when it's time for a closer look.

Periodontal disease is the most common cause of persistent bad breath in dogs. It develops as tartar builds up on the teeth and eventually affects the ligament holding each tooth in place.

The smell can become particularly strong and rotten as the disease progresses. Other signs include inflamed or bleeding gums, loose or missing teeth, heavy tartar, exposed tooth roots, changes in appetite, difficulty chewing, and pawing at the mouth.

Gingivitis is an earlier stage of periodontal disease and causes the gums to become inflamed. Bad breath is often one of the first noticeable signs.

Unlike more advanced periodontal disease, gingivitis is reversible when treated. A professional dental cleaning combined with regular dental care at home can usually address the problem. Without treatment, however, gingivitis can progress into periodontal disease and eventually contribute to tooth loss.

Sometimes the mouth isn't where the problem starts. Digestive conditions can also affect the way a dog's breath smells.

Gastroenteritis, acid reflux, food intolerances, intestinal blockages, and even gastrointestinal cancer can all be associated with changes in breath odor. Many of these conditions can cause vomiting, which leaves behind a sharp, sour smell from bile.

Acid reflux can also produce a similar sour odor even when a dog isn't actually vomiting.

What a dog eats can have a noticeable effect on breath. It's perfectly normal for some of the smell of a dog's food to linger after a meal, but certain diets can leave a much stronger odor behind.

Seafood and fish oil supplements, for example, can give a dog's breath a distinctly fishy smell. Dogs that eat feces, whether their own or another animal's, can also develop particularly foul breath afterward. This behavior, known as coprophagia, is unpleasant but fairly common.

Bad breath isn't always caused by the teeth or gums. The oral cavity also includes the jaw bones, tongue, soft palate, and the inside of the cheeks, and problems affecting any of these areas can produce an unpleasant smell.

Injuries can become infected and lead to tissue damage, creating the odor associated with the breakdown of damaged tissue. Tumors can also develop in these areas and may cause similar tissue damage and bad breath.

A sweet or fruity smell coming from a dog's breath can have a very different explanation. In a diabetic dog, it can be a sign of ketoacidosis, a serious complication that occurs when the body doesn't have enough insulin and begins burning fat for energy instead.

This process produces ketones, which can become toxic as they accumulate in the blood. The resulting breath can have a sweet, fruity smell that is sometimes compared with acetone.

Interestingly, not everyone can smell ketones on a dog's breath. Differences in how people perceive smells, including genetic differences in scent perception, may explain why the odor is more noticeable to some people than others.

Kidney disease can give a dog's breath a distinct ammonia-like smell.

Healthy kidneys filter waste products such as urea from the bloodstream so they can be removed from the body through urine. When kidney function is impaired, urea can build up in the blood instead.

That excess urea eventually reacts with saliva and converts to ammonia, producing the distinctive smell that can be noticeable on a dog's breath.

An unpleasant smell coming from a dog's mouth doesn't always originate anywhere near the mouth. In fact, the problem could be at the opposite end!

Impacted or infected anal glands can cause a dog to lick or nibble the area in an attempt to relieve the discomfort. Anal gland fluid often has an intensely fishy smell, and when a dog licks the area, that odor can transfer directly to the mouth and breath.

Persistent bad breath is worth investigating rather than simply trying to cover up the smell. The underlying cause could be as manageable as dental disease, but it can also be associated with more serious health problems.

Regular brushing and professional dental cleanings can help prevent periodontal disease, which is the most common cause of ongoing bad breath in dogs.

A sudden change in breath odor deserves particular attention, especially if it appears alongside other changes such as appetite problems, vomiting, or repeated licking at a particular part of the body. In those situations, a vet can help determine what's causing the smell and whether anything else needs to be treated.

If you're keen to make nice with the Einstein of the bird world, here's how to go about it...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Is there anything more whimsical, more magical than the idea of being able to befriend a crow?

With the ability to recognize individual people, remember faces and learn from experience, these glossy-feathered birds are among the cleverest birds we're likely to encounter in our gardens. They're also steeped in symbolism, appearing in various traditions as spiritual messengers or guides associated with wisdom, transformation and the mysteries of life.

For those who enjoy looking for a little meaning in the natural world, then, spotting one could feel like more than just another garden bird sighting. Especially if you're the sort of person who obsesses over your birth month bird, or spends ages wondering what the first bird you see each morning says about your day ahead.

Look, we all love finding little stories and connections in nature. Indeed, some of us even believe that the bird we see most in our garden says everything about our gardening style – and a regular crow visitor might suggest there's something rather welcoming about your outdoor space. So, yes, it makes sense many of us are secretly wondering how to befriend a crow.

If you've been on social media lately, you may have stumbled across the (admittedly niche) trend of CrowTok, which sees people share videos of their feathered visitors, the food they leave out and, occasionally, the curious little objects their avian friends appear to bring in return. And while we might like to imagine these offerings are thank-you gifts, there's some fascinating science behind the behaviour.

Yes, the National Audubon Society has explored how crows sometimes leave objects for people who feed them, with corvid biologist John Marzluff explaining that a clever bird could learn that leaving an object results in a tasty reward.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

It's a lovely reminder that our relationship with nature can be full of surprises. Crows are social and remarkably observant birds, and while they're wild animals rather than pets, they can learn to recognise familiar faces and become more comfortable around people who treat them consistently and respectfully.

So, if you'd love to befriend a crow and see a few more of these clever characters dropping by your backyard, there are some simple ways to make your outdoor space more appealing. From offering their favorite snacks to creating a safe spot where they can stop for a drink, here's how to attract crows to your yard – and perhaps even earn their trust in the process.

If there's one way to catch a crow's attention, it's with a tasty snack. Peanuts are a popular choice, and unsalted peanuts are a good option to offer. You could also try a little variety with other suitable foods, such as cooked eggs (plain, obviously, so hold the seasoning!) or mealworms.

It's not just what you offer that matters, however; it's how regularly you do it. Environment for the Americas recommends putting food and water out at the same time and in the same place each day, as crows are intelligent enough to recognise routines, and may soon learn when to expect a visit.

Start by putting out a small amount, then, and clear away anything uneaten to avoid attracting unwanted visitors. With time, your regular visitors may begin to recognize you as the person responsible for their daily delivery.

Crows are naturally cautious birds, so where you put their food can make a big difference if you're trying to make friends with one. Rather than hiding snacks away in a traditional hanging bird feeder, then, try placing a small amount on a low feeding platform or another suitable open surface (like this nifty Deck Bird Feeder from Amazon).

A spot near a fence, shed roof or sturdy tree branch can give them somewhere to perch while they tuck in. And, ideally, you should choose somewhere with clear sightlines, as this allows crows to keep an eye on their surroundings and spot potential danger.

Try to give them plenty of space, too. If you're watching from indoors, they'll have the opportunity to get comfortable with your presence without feeling as though they're being observed too closely.

Food might get their attention, but a reliable source of fresh water can give crows another reason to visit. Try placing a shallow bird bath or sturdy water bowl somewhere accessible, with a gently sloping edge that makes it easy for birds to drink and bathe.

Keep the water fresh, changing it regularly and cleaning the dish to prevent a build-up of dirt and bacteria. Position it somewhere relatively open so visiting crows can watch for potential predators while they stop for a drink... and then get ready for the most tedious part of our How To Befriend A Crow 101 Guide: be patient.

Oh yes, rather than rushing outside to get closer, try sitting quietly at a distance while the birds eat and drink. Some crow enthusiasts on Reddit also suggest making a gentle whistling sound as you put food out, as this helps the birds associate that sound with a reliable food source, but that one is well and truly up to you!

It takes time to befriend a crow. Give it a little while, though, and you may find that your visitors become less wary when you're around. Just let them set the pace – earning the trust of a wild crow is a relationship worth taking slowly.

Sure, you might not end up with a crow delivering shiny little presents to your doorstep, but creating a garden where these intelligent birds feel safe enough to visit? Well, that's a rather lovely reward in itself, I say!

#8209. No Pseudonymity in Ex-Associate's Sexual Assault Claim Against Major Law Firm

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"Permitting Doe to proceed pseudonymously while the Firm defends itself publicly, particularly where there seems to be material factual disputes between the parties, presents an unfair asymmetry that also weighs against anonymity ...."

From Judge W. Scott Hardy in Doe v. Blank Rome LLP, the opinion was issued under seal in May, but just unsealed last week (at my behest):

Plaintiff is an attorney who filed a detailed, 197-paragraph Complaint under the pseudonym "Jane Doe" against Defendant Blank Rome LLP …, her former employer, alleging claims for sex discrimination, hostile work environment, and retaliation pursuant to Title VII …. Her claims arise from the Firm's purported failure to respond appropriately after Doe allegedly was sexually assaulted by another associate attorney, identified in the Complaint as "Associate A," while they and others were socializing at the home of a Firm partner on a Saturday evening after leaving a graduation party hosted by another partner of the Firm. The Complaint details Doe's professional background, including where she attended law school, when she began her employment at the Firm, and the type of law she practiced while at the Firm.

Doe's Complaint similarly details Associate A's professional background, including his law school and year of graduation, and the names of his prior law firms. The Complaint does not identify Doe by her own name, nor does it identify by name "Associate A" or any other attorney at the Firm. The only person identified by name in the Complaint is the Firm's Chief Human Resource Officer, who is named 24 times….

The court noted the strong presumption in favor of parties litigating in their own names, and concludes this presumption wasn't rebutted here:

A mere showing of embarrassment or economic harm is not enough [to justify pseudonymity]. Rather, there must be a showing of both: (1) fear of severe harm, and (2) that the fear of severe harm is reasonable. When a litigant sufficiently alleges that he or she has a reasonable fear of severe harm from litigating without a pseudonym, the Third Circuit instructs that "district courts should balance the plaintiff's interest and fear against the public's strong interest in an open litigation process." {"[T]he Court is sympathetic to Plaintiff's concerns, and understands that, unfortunately, victims of sexual harassment and assault often face ridicule and further harassment when they file lawsuits or otherwise publicly disclose their allegations, especially in the internet age. However, these concerns, while certainly reasonable, are not sufficient to outweigh the public's right to access court proceedings."} …

It also expressed its concern about one-sided pseudonymity (a concern that some courts weigh heavily and others don't, as this article lays out in detail):

Doe is not the only party exposed to public humiliation and reputational harm. The Firm itself and its chief human resource officer have been identified publicly in the Complaint (and other current or former Firm attorneys have been described with sufficient identifying indicia in the Complaint to be identified by implication). Permitting Doe to proceed pseudonymously while the Firm defends itself publicly, particularly where there seems to be material factual disputes between the parties, presents an unfair asymmetry that also weighs against anonymity ….

Doe … plead[ed] highly detailed factual averments in her 197-paragraph Complaint that inform the reader of her law school, her prior law firm affiliation, the month and year she commenced work at the Firm, the general nature of her practice, and the date of her departure from the Firm. Similar factual averments were plead regarding Associate A, including by naming three firms at which Associate A had previously been employed. The Firm's identity has also been revealed both in the caption of the Complaint and in its detailed factual averments. Many of these averments supply indicia of identity of both Doe and Associate A even though they would not have been necessary pursuant to applicable pleading standards set forth in Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)…. [This] weighs against anonymity.

The court also mentioned Doe's argument "that there are social stigmas that attach to victims of sexual assault and harassment, and that using her real name would subject her to 'ridicule, scrutiny, and alienation' by her own colleagues and would jeopardize her reputation within the local legal community," but responded that (1) "Doe is an adult, not a minor" and that (2) she "does not contend that she would forgo her claims if her motion to proceed pseudonymously were to be denied and there is no indication from the record that Doe would be deterred from proceeding if she identified herself." For whatever it's worth, plaintiff dismissed the case a few months after the decision denying pseudonymity, presumably pursuant to a settlement. Because of the dismissal, neither Doe nor Associate A were publicly identified in the docket.

Finally, the court discussed in some detail the question "whether either party stakes out their respective positions here for illegitimate ulterior motives," a factor that some courts' multi-factor tests for pseudonymity mention but that rarely gets much elaboration:

Doe contends that the Firm would have no reason for opposing her motion other than her bald accusation that such opposition is being undertaken to "perpetuate ongoing harm" and to "further humiliate her, undermine her professional reputation and potentially deter her form continuing with this litigation." Doe proffers no particularized basis for this accusation beyond her objection that the Firm's General Counsel circulated an internal communication within the Firm itself about Doe at or near the time her Complaint was filed, to contend that the Firm opposes her pending motion for illegitimate and "nefarious" motives, further suggesting the Firm is opposing it as a "litigation tacti[c]."

For its part, the Firm similarly accuses Doe of illegitimate tactical motives for seeking to proceed pseudonymously despite filing a factually detailed Complaint with enough content for a reader to know or surmise the identities of its personnel so that she may "cast[] aspersions upon the character of others about whom she publicly alleges information that makes them readily identifiable." The Court notes, too, that Doe filed her detailed Complaint without seeking leave to file it under seal or in redacted form and did file it on the public docket approximately a week before seeking to proceed pseudonymously. {In saying so, the Court is not suggesting that proceeding in this manner is inappropriate or that that seeking to file such a pleading under seal or in redacted form is the better course. Though, there may be circumstances when doing so is advisable.}

On the present record, the Court discerns no illegitimate or nefarious motives by either party. In reaching this conclusion, the Court notes that there are known and anticipated vicissitudes and adversities to litigants involved in presumptively public judicial proceedings.

Here, the Defendant is a large, multi-office law firm and Doe is one of its former lawyers. Both parties are experienced with the judiciary and presumably familiar with the reasonably foreseeable extrajudicial consequences litigation has on parties and witnesses.

Moreover, lawyers representing their clients in court, such as counsel of record here, are expected to prepare and file pleadings and briefs on court dockets for legitimate purposes that subject them to potential sanctions if such filings are presented for an improper purpose. Of course, pleadings and briefs having a proper purpose may also have attendant collateral adverse extrajudicial consequences, but such consequences do not necessarily transform a proper filing into an improper one. Sometimes those boundaries are clear, sometimes blurred. {Here, on the present record, the Court detects some potential tactical and strategic efforts by both parties within the context of otherwise legitimate and proper lawyering but cautions both parties and their counsel to stay within those boundaries going forward.}

As noted above, Doe has a legitimate interest in seeking to proceed pseudonymously to avoid potential embarrassment, humiliation, emotional distress, and professional reputational harm. Those are reasonable and understandable concerns. Likewise, the Firm's opposition to Doe's request is grounded on the desire for symmetry in the transparency of the Court's administration of justice so that Doe may not be permitted to "hurl accusations … from behind 'a cloak of anonymity.'" The Court agrees that such rationale, rooted in fairness and tethered to the presumption of transparency in court proceedings, is also reasonable and legitimate. Accordingly, the parties' respective motives neither favor nor disfavor Doe's continued anonymity.

And the court concluded by noting "the presumption in favor of open judicial proceedings," and by saying that, "[w]hile the parties here are not public officials or public bodies, the strong presumption in favor of open judicial proceedings is not outweighed by the other … factors considered above."

NEXT: Today in Supreme Court History: November 16, 1939

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

Domestic cats are descended from African desert wild cats. These wild felines got most of their hydration from their prey. Their kidneys became ultra-efficient at retaining moisture, and their drive to find fresh water sources nearly disappeared completely.

Our house cats retain this same physiology and lack of interest in hunting down fresh water. The problem? They arenât typically chowing down on juicy rodents a dozen times a day. Which means they often donât get the moisture they need to keep those specialized kidneys healthy.

This is why 40% of cats over 10 years old and 80% of cats over 15 years old develop chronic kidney disease. After a lifetime of chronic dehydration, their kidneys simply canât keep up.

One solution is to increase the amount of water cats consume through their food by offering wet food or adding water to their dry food. This is doable if you are home during meal times every day. But if you work long hours, have a million other things to juggle, or occasionally (or often) travel, feeding moist meals consistently becomes more of a challenge.

Some turn to automatic wet food feeders that keep pre-prepared portions of wet food cool, automatically opening each portion on a set schedule. While these work in the short term, they hold only a limited amount of food (generally between three and six meals) and require a lot of cleanup and constant restocking.

For those who travel or already struggle to get everything done in a day, this is far from being a convenient or effective solution.

The Neakasa Riko Fresh-Made Wet Meal Feeder combines the health benefits of a wet-food diet with the convenience and high-capacity of a dry-food automatic feeder.

Unlike traditional automatic wet food feeders that can only store a handful of meals, the Neakasa Riko Fresh-Made Wet Meal Feeder can hold weeks of food at a time and dispense meals up to every hour, keeping kitties with even the most specialized dietary needs happy and hydrated throughout the day.

Rather than canned or wet packaged food, the Riko works with freeze-dried cat food. This shelf-stable food is ground up into portions, mixed with water, and allowed to rehydrate before serving.

No refrigeration or constant refilling needed. Just fill the hopper with a bag of freeze-dried food of your choice, add filtered water to the reservoir, set the amounts and feeding schedule on the app, and take a well-deserved break from fretting over your catâs meals and hydration status.

Neakasa is a smart-home and pet-care brand operated by Genhigh, a technology company headquartered in Shenzhen, China. Founded in 2017 as Neabot, the company specializes in automated solutions designed to make everyday home and pet care easier, including robotic cleaning and smart pet products. The Riko is manufactured in China, where the company is based.

Given the price point of this product, I wouldnât recommend it to cat owners simply hoping to unload some of their kitty chores to automation. There are less expensive automatic feeders for that. But for cat owners who normally feed wet food but are taking a long trip or frequently travel and want a feeder that can provide meals more often than their cat sitter can, the Riko Wet Meal Feeder is a worthwhile investment.

It is also a great option for cats who require small portions frequently throughout the day or who already eat freeze-dried food and can benefit from a more consistent schedule and more moisture in their diet.

Because this feeder allows for highly customized feeding routines and portions, it works well for kittens, adults, and seniors. But do be aware that the meal sizes cap out at 15g of dried food, which means larger cats may require multiple feedings throughout the day rather than the typical two meals they might be used to, something the app makes easy.

The Neakasa Riko takes the guesswork out of serving moistened meals. Simply fill the food hopper with compatible freeze-dried food, fill the water tank, and use the app to create a feeding schedule.

At mealtime, Riko automatically grinds the food, adds your selected amount of water, and allows the mixture to soak while the bowl is hidden out of reach. Once the food is ready, the bowl swings out so your cat can enjoy their fresh meal.

You can adjust the water-to-food ratio to create a consistency your cat prefers, from thicker to more soupy. Riko can schedule multiple meals throughout the day, add water to keep uneaten food fresh, and track food consumption through the app.

Beyond preparing moistened meals, the Riko packs several thoughtful features into the feeder itself:

Large capacity: The 3-liter food hopper and 2.4-liter water tank can hold enough for 10+ days of feeding.

Freshness-focused design: An airtight food compartment, desiccant system, and sealed grinder help protect freeze-dried food from moisture.

Precise portions: Riko weighs each serving for approximately Â±1-gram portioning.

Easy cleaning: The removable stainless-steel bowl is dishwasher-safe, while other components can be removed for cleaning. Each order comes with two bowls, so you can pop one in the dishwasher while the other is in use.

The Neakasa app gives you control over Riko from your phone, whether youâre home or away. You can create feeding schedules, adjust portion sizes and water-to-food ratios, and trigger extra meals remotely.

The app also records your catâs food and water intake, making it easier to spotchanges in eating habits over time. Youâll receive alerts for low food and water storage and potential feeding problems, while adjustable settings let you configure features such as freshness detection, child lock, and desiccant replacement reminders.

Through the app, you have control over the amount of ground food in each meal, the ratio of water added, how long it sits to rehydrate, and how often water is added if food is left over. You can even program âwater onlyâ meals to encourage even more moisture intake.

Riko can be customized with a few optional accessories. The rechargeable battery pack provides up to seven days of cordless operation and backup power during outages, while the Multi-Cat Access Module uses microchip recognition to restrict feeding to each designated cat in multi-cat households.

Neakasa also sells replacement silicone desiccant packs with a color-changing indicator that lets you know when the pack needs replacing.

Number of meals per fill: 3 daysâ worth

Compatible with: all types of canned food

If youâve read any of my reviews before, then you know that my cat, Makoa, is a BIG fan of food. So any device that makes meal times less of a hassle for me and more accessible for him is worth trying out. And, since our family also travels fairly frequently, I thought this high-tech contraption might be helpful in multiple ways.

When the Riko arrived, I immediately felt like I was unboxing some kind of fancy kitty espresso maker! Itâs about the same size as one, and the grinder really does look very similar to a coffee grinder.

Getting the Riko set up was fairly painless. I followed the Quick Start Instructions to assemble the few parts that had been stored internally during shipping, then downloaded the app and connected the device to my Wi-Fi.

From there, things got a touch trickier. Because the Riko works using weight, not volume, it can be a little difficult to set the proportions for each meal. For example, I typically feed Makoa Â¼ cup twice per day. How many grams of ground freeze-dried food plus water is that? No idea.

Luckily, the app does have a very helpful Smart Feeding Plan setup that allows you to use your catâs weight and select the type of food you feed to automatically create a feeding schedule based on the food brand's recommended intake.

The downside here is that it defaults to 10 meals per day. Which probably isnât a bad thing since cats did evolve to eat multiple small meals throughout the day (and this also guarantees better hydration). But if your cat is used to a couple of big meals at the same time each day, this can make for a tough transition.

I ended up manually adding up the dry food total it recommended, then manually adding meals that were more aligned with his typical schedule.

The other hangup I ran into is that the feeder (in the US, at least) maxes out at 15g of ground food per meal. For comparison, my 12-pound cat needs about 60g of ground food per day. In other words, I had to schedule at least four meals per day for him to get all the food he needs.

These smaller meal sizes are intentional. Not only does it help avoid food being wasted (or left out for too long without being eaten), but it also ensures your cat is continually taking in food-based moisture throughout the dayâthe way they evolved to.

So I wouldnât say this is a bad thing or design flaw, but it is something you and your cat may need to adjust to.

Beyond the tricky parts of portioning and scheduling, I really do love this feeder! It is so easy to fill and, once the schedule is set, you really can just forget it. It starts preparing each meal ahead of time so that the food is ready at the scheduled mealtime.

It makes a recognizable beep when food is ready, so your cat can learn to come as soon as dinner is served. (Makoa learned to recognize the low buzz of the grinder almost instantly, and now waits for his meals twenty minutes before they are served.)

Not only has this gadget taken the stress off me (now Makoa has something else to obsess over when itâs dinner time), but it has made it so much easier to ensure consistent, moist meals throughout the day. And I know it will be a lifesaver for those weekend trips and long vacations our family likes to go on.

I highly recommend this feeder to anyone who is looking for a way to automate their catâs meals without having to rely on dry kibble. The rehydrated freeze-dried food isnât the same as canned food, but the texture is similar, and most cats love this type of food, especially when it is mixed with water. Even better, freeze-dried food tends to be healthier and more nutrient-dense than even the best canned food options.

No. Riko is designed to grind and rehydrate freeze-dried food, not conventional wet food. Do not put canned, pouch, or other wet food, or kibble, dehydrated, or air-dried food into the hopper.

Because Riko adds water to the food before serving, the resulting meal should be treated like wet food. Neakasa recommends that your cat consume it within about three to four hours.

Riko's freshness settings can detect leftover food and pause the next scheduled feeding when the amount remaining exceeds your chosen threshold. The feeder can also retract the bowl after food has remained uneaten for an extended period.

If hydration is a concern for your cat and providing consistent moist food is a challenge for you, then the Neakasa Riko is worth looking into.

This high-tech automatic feeder can store 10 days' worth of freeze-dried food at a time and provide up to 20 freshly rehydrated meals per day. Each meal can be scheduled and proportioned to meet your catâs needs while ensuring their moisture intake is optimal to avoid future health issues. It's perfect for busy cat parents, extended periods away, and cats who require frequent, moistened meals.

#8207. If Life With Dogs Were a Movie, These Would Be the Outtakes

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Meet Dave Coverly, creator of the popular cartoon panel, âSpeed Bumpâ, which appears internationally in hundreds of publications, including The Washington Post, the Los Angeles Times, and the Detroit Free Press. His work was named âBest in Newspaper Panelsâ by the National Cartoonists Society in 1995, 2003, 2014, and 2021. He is also the principal cartoonist for Bark (formerly BarkBox) and illustrator for Ranger Rick magazine.

We sit down with Dave to learn the story behind his charmingly wry comic, and find out how, 32 years down the road, inspiration in the ordinary keeps his content relevant and relatable.

The path to becoming a professional cartoonist always starts in childhood â pretty much every kid likes to draw, right? And I was no different. But as kids get older, they tend to get more particular about how good their drawings look, and thatâs where frustration sets in. They tend to move on to other hobbies. Where a cartoonistâs path diverges from that of wiser, more sensible humans is that we love the process of creating more than we chafe at the frustration. Believe me, there is frustration. One misconception about artists is that we do it because it comes easy to us, but the general truth is that most of us put in long hours because we want to be good at what we already love.

I taped rejection letters to the wall above my drawing table for motivation. At the time, though, my panels didnât have a title, so when my breakthrough finally happened, I needed to name it. I submitted a list of possible titles to Creators, and Speed Bump was the unanimous choice. Fortunately, that was my top choice, too. Iâd like people to perhaps slow down just for a second when they read my work since Iâm rarely going to hit you over the head with the joke.

My second favorite title was The Wide World of Stretch Pants.

Animal humor has always been a part of my work. I was slightly obsessed with Ranger Rick magazine growing up, and spent loads of time drawing the critters they featured. I discovered thereâs something inherently funny and absurd about talking animals, not to mention itâs the most fun way to trigger the imagination. What would a giraffe order at a restaurant? What does a dolphin dream about? That was how I discovered how much fun cartooning was â and that the crazier you make it, the less perfect it needs to be.

Iâve always had a dog until very recently, and had two hilarious knuckleheads as a kid: Shag and Tigger. They were actually father and son, and I didnât need a DNA test to prove it â Shag got out one day, and the neighborhood kids on bikes came by to let me know he could be found down the street at Queenieâs house, where they were in the front yard together. Letâs just say Shag was living up to his name. Then Queenie begat Tigger.

I grew up in a small lake community, but Shag was found by my grandpa just living on the streets of Detroit. He was pretty feral â Shag, not my grandpa â and impossible to train, but also a total sweetheart. They slept in the garage, and in the morning weâd often find him sleeping on top of the car. Tigger, on the other hand, preferred to sleep behind the toilet. And he wasnât a small dog.

In any case, I believe these two funny mutts had as much influence on my work as any other cartoonist.

Great question! Cats and dogs are obviously very different, but they have one really big thing in common: their own unique personalities. Thatâs what makes both perfect for cartoons â most of us already treat them like little furry people anyway, right? Itâs just their behaviors that set them apart.

Dogs tend to be goofier, cats tend to be cooler, and they show affection in their own ways, too. Pets generate a lot of material because almost everyone knows a dog or a cat. Even if they donât have one (or many) themselves, the odds are a reader will recognize why the cartoon is funny (hopefully!).

One of my most popular cartoons is a sign that says âBeware of Avant-Guard Dog,â and the dog in the yard is wearing black and a beret and holding a sign simply saying WOOF. The idea started as a pun, but I think one of the reasons readers seem to like it so much is that it plays against type. The dogâs sensibility is quite cat-like, making it even more absurd.

My new book is a full-color collection of the âbest ofâ my dog cartoons from the last decade, and thereâs only one cartoon per page so that they can be seen in a larger format, which was important to me. I put a lot of effort into the art and the details, things that are often lost when the cartoons are shrunk down to an illegible size, so I wanted readers to be able to fully enjoy that aspect of the cartoons. Also, the friend who colors my panels, Ron Raff, is a genius, so whether you think the jokes are funny or not, youâll see that they look gorgeous and consistent throughout!

It was difficult but fun to choose which cartoons made the cut, too. Some are simply personal favorites; others were chosen based on readersâ reactions and how much love they got online. Feedback is extremely helpful, by the way â sometimes it feels like Iâm drawing these alone in my belfry studio and tossing them into a black hole, so hearing from people which ones they liked really makes my day.

There are two aspects to dog cartoons: The first and most obvious is that they really arejokes about dogsâ behavior in general â how they eat, how they might react in different settings, why they lick themselves, bathroom habits, etc etc. Thereâs a lot of material there! The second aspect is what generates even more material, and thatâs when dogs are reflecting human behavior, or simply behaving like a human.

Many of the dog cartoons are really about us, and heaven knows people will never stop providing fodder for jokes. Dogs â and animals in general â are a good buffer between the joke and the point of the joke. A good example in the book is a dog shaking a toy in his mouth, and a woman next to him is saying, âBad dog! Drop Mommyâs voodoo doll! Bad dog!â In the background, her husband (presumably) shakes back and forth like the toy. At some level, the cartoon is about the coupleâs relationship, right? But itâs framed by a typical and humorous dog action weâve all seen before. Just not with a voodoo doll, haha.

I would say simply that our question is also the answer: love. I try to approach my cartoons the same way I approach dogs in real life; from a standpoint of love, affection, admiration, and a little bit of gratitude that they exist.

There have been too many to count over three decades! I drew a cartoon years ago of a man walking his dog in heaven, but the leash is attached to the dogâs halo. A few weeks later, I received a card in the mail from a woman whose dog had just passed awayâ¦only a month after her husband. She said she cried with happiness thinking of the two of them like that, and it made her heart feel lighter. How incredibly moving is that? I think of that often: when I share a cartoon, the reader brings their own life experiences to it and then weâve made a two-way connection. That connection is my favorite part of the gig.

My only hope is that my cartoons help people simply see the world in a different way for a few seconds. I want them to laugh with others and not at others; see that absurdities are universal and that when we recognize ourselves or others in a cartoon, weâre really just acknowledging that weâre all connected.

And then I hope they cut them out and slap them on their fridges.

The best place to find all my work and links is my site: www.speedbump.com, and anyone should feel free to reach out, follow, etc on Instagram (https://www.instagram.com/speedbumpcomic/) or Facebook (https://www.facebook.com/davecoverly)

If youâre a skywriter, aim for the west side of Ann Arbor. Iâll look out the skylight in my belfry studio.

#8205. Thinking About Adopting A Dog? Here Are 5 Things To Ask Before Bringing Them Home

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

This article was created in sponsorship with Mars, which helps make content like this possible.

Adopting can be one of the most rewarding ways to welcome a new pet into your life. But for many would-be adopters, the biggest hurdle isnât necessarily that they don't want to adopt; it's feeling confident that theyâre making an informed and responsible decision.

Mars research found that while 58% of pet owners have never adopted from a shelter or rescue organization, nearly a third would consider it with the right support available. Whether you have concerns about a pet's medical and behavior history, or understanding what to feed them, there are lots of questions to consider before welcoming a new dog into your home.

Mars is #ClearingThePath to pet adoption by giving prospective and new dog owners access to practical, expert-backed support throughout the journey.

Responsible adoption is about more than picking the right dog; it's about making sure you can realistically meet their needs. Before adopting, think about your living space, daily routine, work arrangements, and how much time you can dedicate to helping your new dog settle in and meeting their exercise, enrichment, and training needs.

Surprising for some, living in an apartment, for example, does not automatically mean you cannot adopt a dog. The right match depends less on the size of your home and more on whether you can meet that individual dogâs physical, mental, and social needs.

Always mention if you have existing pets or children at the beginning of the adoption process too. Shelter staff can help identify pets whose personality, energy level, and other needs may be a good fit for family life.

The more you speak honestly and openly with the shelter about your home, family, and daily routine, the more they can help you understand which dog will be the right match.

Moving from a shelter into a home is a huge change for your new best friend, and youâd be amazed by how many dogs are returned to shelters within their first few days, before theyâve even had a chance to decompress, let alone adjust to their new situation.

A useful way to think about the transition is the â3-3-3â guideline: the first three days, three weeks, and three months.

During the first three days, your dog may feel overwhelmed. Dogs may hide, sleep more than usual, show less interest in food, or simply seem unsure of their surroundings. Some dogs may even show signs of fear or defensiveness, and itâs important to understand that this is not necessarily their true personality.

Keep things calm and predictable, and let your dog set the pace.

Once they become more comfortable, you may start seeing more of their personality from around three weeks, and this can be a good time to introduce gentle routines, socialization, and basic training. By around three months, many dogs may feel much more at home, although every pet is different, so donât worry if your dog seems to need longer. Just be patient and give them the time and space they need to feel safe.

Mars research found that 71% of adopters change their petâs diet immediately after adoption. However, switching your new dogâs food right away may not be the best option, even if their previous diet wasnât the best quality. Ask the shelter what your dog currently eats, how much they are fed, and how often. Keeping their existing food and routine initially can help reduce unnecessary disruption.

If you want to change their food, wait a week or so to allow them to adjust, then do so gradually by adding a small proportion of the new diet to the dogâs regular diet. On the first day, their old food should make up around three-quarters of the meal, with the new food making up the rest.

Puppies in particular need age-appropriate nutrition to support growth and should not be switched onto adult food too early.

A dogâs diet should be complete and balanced for their age, size, activity level, body condition and health needs, and plenty of fresh water should always be available.

Consistency can help your dog understand their new environment and build trust.

Establish regular times for meals, walks, rest, and play. As your dog becomes more comfortable, you can begin introducing basic training using positive reinforcement. Keep sessions short, fun, and rewarding.

Itâs normal for there to be some bumps along the way as your dog adjusts to a new home and routine. Behaviors they had previously learned â toilet training, for example â may temporarily change while they settle in, so patience and consistency are important.

If you notice any sudden, persistent, or concerning changes in behavior, speak to your veterinarian or a qualified behavior professional for advice.

Adopting and bringing a new dog home is just the beginning, and itâs completely normal for questions to come up as they settle into a new routine. If you need extra guidance regarding their behavior, health, nutrition, or day-to-day care, donât be afraid to reach out. Your shelter, veterinarian, or a qualified behavior professional can help you understand the right way forward.

For more advice to help you prepare for adoption and support your dog once theyâre home, visit the Mars Adoption Hub.
