#8203. School Board Member Seeks "Better Sense of How" Church "Approaches Issues of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Around Their Messaging" …

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"around some key issues relevant to marginalized communities," including as to "the Church's views on same-sex marriage, '[a]ccess to safe and affordable abortion,' '[a]ccess to gender affirming medical care,' '[c]onversion therapy for LGBTQIA+ individuals (youth and adults),' and '[i]nclusive sexual education and access to birth control for youth.'"

This happened when the board was deciding whether to allow a long-term lease of space on weekends to a church, pursuant to a policy that allowed such leases for community groups generally. And, a federal court held Friday, this violated the First Amendment. Some excerpts from the long opinion in Pines Church v. Hermon School Dep't, by Chief Judge Lance Walker (D. Me.):

Plaintiff Matt Gioia moved his family from Colorado to Maine in the summer of 2020 to start a new church. Gioia was born in Waterville, Maine, and lived in Guilford, Maine until he graduated high school and joined the military at seventeen years old. Initially, Gioia's church—The Pines Church—gathered at his home. In March of 2021, The Pines Church began holding Sunday morning services at a movie theater in Orono, Maine, pursuant to a month-to-month lease arrangement. As the Church grew, Gioia began to look for a new space that could accommodate a larger group.

Gioia sought space from the Hermon School Department, which generally opens up its facilities to various groups:

This policy provides that "[s]chool facilities should be made available for appropriate community use when such facilities are not required for their primary purposes: the instruction of students and related school activities." The policy distinguishes between "occasional or short-term use of school facilities," which "shall be authorized by the school principal," and "long-term rental or lease," which "shall be authorized by the Hermon School Committee upon the recommendation of the Superintendent of Schools."

But the Hermon School Committee (which consisted of "Committee Chair Jesse Keith, Vice Chair Karen Shorey, Stephanie Oiler, Haily Keezer, and Christopher McLaughlin") denied the Church's request for a year-long or six-month lease, allowing only a month-to-month lease (which appeared to be inadequate for the church, given its need for a stable meeting location). Here's part of the summary of the facts, based on the bench trial that the court held:

The next day [after a hearing], a former committee member emailed Keith and Shorey to share her belief "that it is not in our communities [sic] best interest to lease one of our school facilities to any religious organization," warning that "[t]here is a quiet movement in our country by some conservative religious groups who are actively working to soften the boundaries between church/state, starting with our schools" and that granting the Church a lease would lead to "a slippery slope." She wondered how the Hermon School Department would have to respond to a similar request from "an Imam who wants to open a mosque," in light of the "precedent" set by a lease to The Pines Church.

Her email concluded with unintended irony: "There's a reason why the founding fathers wrote the constitution the way they did." Keith and Shorey denied at trial that this email influenced their decision-making with respect to the Church's lease request, which I find implausible in light of the trial record….

McLaughlin reached out to [HSD Superintendent Micah] Grant and explained that he "had a few additional questions" for Gioia:

McLaughlin "wanted to get a better sense of how [T]he Pines Church approaches issues of diversity, equity, and inclusion around their messaging around some key issues relevant to marginalized communities." Those questions requested information about the Church's views on same-sex marriage, "[a]ccess to safe and affordable abortion," "[a]ccess to gender affirming medical care," "[c]onversion therapy for LGBTQIA+ individuals (youth and adults)," and "[i]nclusive sexual education and access to birth control for youth." …

[At a later meeting, High School Principal Brian] Walsh took the podium and explained that he had several reservations about the Church's request. He first explained that it would be difficult to find the staff to clean the building on Sunday afternoons. But apart from this, he continued:

[W]e've never had a long-term lease, at least over my twenty-one years here, and I think there's a number of reasons we don't do that. There's a lot of variables we just don't know. No question our students should come first, our program should come first.

We also don't know or have the sense of how this will be promoted, to [the student representative's] question. If you put Hermon High School's name with a church or another organization with different beliefs than the school has, I see that as problematic. But again, that's where I sit and that's where I stand. Doesn't mean this organization won't do a great job, doesn't mean they won't support, hopefully, our mission as well. I just don't know, there are too many variables with that and again we have not—we have never done that.

What I would not want is for students to feel like a group organization that we are renting to, their vision or their mission is now ours. And there's a blurred line when it comes to that. I have nothing against this church, this reverend, or anything, we've just never said yes to something like this, so probably why it's in your hands, because you guys get to make that decision. I'm looking at the facility and some other variables, so that's kind of—that's where I come from….

[At a later meeting,] Oiler then made a motion for a month-to-month lease, citing concerns about the number of people and cleaning the space afterwards, which she was careful to emphasize had nothing to do with the organization. Keezer asked if they could ask Gioia about how the Church kept its current space clean. Oiler curiously protested that this was not about the Church (when in fact it was ostensibly about the Church and its janitorial readiness) but any organization, then adding the less than persuasive point that if fifteen people got the stomach bug at the same time, someone would have to clean it up. {At trial, Oiler testified that she had in mind a specific incident that occurred at Hermon Middle School when one of her children was a student there.}

Given the shortage of custodial staffing, she explained, she was concerned about the number of people who would be coming in and out of the building. She suggested that the Committee investigate its current rental arrangements, to make sure those organizations were paying what they should considering the costs associated with hosting them. What this had to do with the Church's application remains a mystery….

The Free Speech Clause prohibits restrictions on access to limited or designated public fora that "discriminate against speech on the basis of viewpoint," including on the basis that the viewpoint in question is a religious one. In other words, if a public school's facilities are available for public use, a religious organization cannot be denied access to those facilities because it is a religious organization. Similarly, the Free Exercise Clause "bars even 'subtle departures from neutrality' on matters of religion," and therefore prohibits "denying a generally available benefit solely on account of religious identity," unless such denial is "justified … by a state interest 'of the highest order.'" …

By virtue of Policy KG, the Hermon School Department made its facilities available "for appropriate community use when such facilities are not required for their primary purposes: the instruction of students and related school activities," including for "long-term rental or lease." Having done so, the School Department could not then reject the Church's lease application because it is a religious organization or because of disagreement with its religious viewpoints, without violating the First Amendment, as Plaintiffs contend has occurred….

The court concluded that the Department indeed violate the Church's First Amendment rights, by discriminating against it based on its "religious viewpoint or out of animus against that viewpoint":

I start with the question of whether a majority or significant block of committee members demonstrated bad motive.

I find without any difficulty that McLaughlin exhibited bad motive. McLaughlin's intrusive questions expressed viewpoint related concerns towards Plaintiffs, and he was the only member not to vote in favor of any lease term, including the month-to-month arrangement. Although his email itemizing political and cultural questions occurred early in the process, before the Committee received any advice from counsel, and even though he testified that he harbored no ill will toward Plaintiffs after gaining more information about them, it strikes me as very likely that McLaughlin lacked objectivity when it came to the question of leasing school space to the Church.

It appears that he based his decision directly on the Plaintiffs' religious beliefs and its associated political and culture ethics that flow from those beliefs, and the religious nature of the proposed use. McLaughlin would have approached a lease request differently had it been presented by an organization that shared his personal beliefs.

I also find that Oiler was unable to overcome concerns over constitutionally permissible school-church association, notwithstanding the legal advice the Committee received, and Grant repeatedly emphasized. Though less openly hostile than McLaughlin, Oiler's attitude toward the Church was anything but neutral…. [I]t struck me during her testimony, and I find, that Oiler's chief concern was that the tenant would be a Church. This was made only more obvious by protesting far too much that this was not about the Church but instead fear, for example, of mass vomiting epidemics and the platoon of janitorial assistance that would be required to mop it up.

All of her other concerns about space and the like were definitively answered by Grant as not remotely problematic. I find based on the trial record that her motive was to avoid the School's association with the Church for its religious views. The First Amendment is designed to avoid discriminatory treatment of religious organizations in their enjoyment of the benefits of public facilities based on their religious beliefs or speech. For this reason, I find that Oiler, like McLaughlin, voted as she did based on "bad motive."

I find that Plaintiffs have proved that bad motive prevented Shorey from approaching the lease question fairly. Shorey, at her deposition, suggested that she believed McLaughlin's culture war email was appropriate, even though she later sought to characterize it as inappropriate at trial.

It may be that Shorey believes that a School Committee should have the discretion to question any organization about how its values align with what she sees as the school community's values, to the extent a school community has its own conflicting body of values that can be reduced to a catechesis—perhaps it does. But support for a process that involves examining a prospective tenant's views on religious issues, simply because the prospective tenant is a church, tends rather starkly to highlight the questioner's lack of neutrality toward religion….

Although I find that a majority of voting members exhibited bad motive which would itself be sufficient to end the inquiry, my findings should be considered also in context of the discussion during the deliberative process, which included rather openly anti-religious organization sentiment expressed by Walsh at least as he served as a voice of the school community and the discomfort it might experience especially if the beliefs of the School, whatever those might be, and the Church were at loggerheads. Even if the record had not established a majority of voting members acting out of bad motive, it would still have constituted a significant bloc of legislators and "circumstances suggesting the probable complicity of others," as well as "evidence indicating that the legislators bowed to an impermissible community animus."

Recall that Walsh passed along student concerns about the Church qua church using the School and when asked if any spoke supportively of the idea, Walsh reported that none had. Also recall the email received by Keith Shorey from a former committee member. That former member insisted that this was all a Trojan horse coordinated by conservative Christian groups to blur the line between school and religion. What would the Committee do, the former committee member queried, if an Imam were to set up shop at Hermon High School next?

The standard is one of likelihood, and on that basis, I find that at least three of the five decision makers acted under the influence of bad motive and in so doing violated the Plaintiffs' rights under the First Amendment….

Defendant points to the majority vote in favor of a month-to-month use arrangement as proof of the lack of bias on the part of its committee members. I agree with the Church that this was not persuasive evidence of a lack of bad motive but to the contrary, is evidence of bad motive. The Committee knew the Church required a more fixed arrangement before uprooting itself from its then current location than a month-to-month arrangement provides. This appears to me to have been an offer designed to be rejected not one born of wholesome support for the Free Exercise Clause….

Bethany Onishenko and Robert H. Tyler (Tyler Law LLP), Erin Mersino and Julianne E. Fleischer (Advocates for Faith and Freedom), Joel L. Oster (Oster Law Firm), Wenonah Wirick (Conley & Wirick, P.A.) represent plaintiffs.

What a hoot! If Bieber's garden visitor has left you wishing for an owl of your own, here's how to make your yard more inviting.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Baby, baby, baby, oh! Justin Bieber might not be a name we'd usually associate with gardening, but the singer's latest Instagram photo dump has certainly given us food for thought.

Among the snapshots was a glimpse of what looks like a rather dreamy outdoor living space, complete with cozy terrace sofas, an outdoor fireplace and even an outdoor TV screen. But it was another, slightly blurrier photograph that caught this writer's attention: an owl, seemingly a great horned owl (aka the birth month owl for January babies everywhere!), paying a visit to his garden.

A post shared by Justin Bieber (@lilbieber)

Naturally, this isn't Bieber's first foray into the world of owl appreciation. The singer has had an owl tattoo on his forearm since 2012, with the bird representing wisdom – so it's easy to assume that this latest garden visitor was a particularly welcome sight for him.

Now, Justin Bieber certainly isn't alone in his fascination with these magnificent birds of prey. Whether it's their haunting calls, striking eyes or wonderfully mysterious reputation, there's something rather special about spotting an owl close to home.

So, if Bieber's feathered visitor has left you wondering how to welcome one of these beautiful birds into your own backyard, the good news is that there are a few things you can do to make your yard more owl-friendly.

One of the best ways to encourage owls into your yard à la Justin Bieber is to give them somewhere safe to nest. Depending on the species in your area, then, installing an owl box could provide just the inviting home they're looking for.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

The trick is to figure out which owls are visiting before you buy (or DIY) your nesting box; eastern screech owls, for example, are cavity nesters and will readily use suitably sized nesting boxes. Great horned owls, on the flipside, typically use open nests rather than enclosed boxes.

Once you've researched the requirements of your local owl species, all that's left to do is position your new nesting box high up in a mature tree, somewhere quiet and away from too much human activity.

A perfectly manicured lawn might look lovely, but a slightly wilder yard? Why, that could be much more appealing to visiting owls, as tese birds of prey need somewhere to hunt. (A healthy population of small mammals, such as mice and voles, can provide an important food source).

Try leaving a patch of grass a little longer, planting native grasses and wildflowers, and preserving mature trees wherever possible. Trees offer useful perching and roosting spots (something like the ‘Temple of Bloom’ Seven-Son from Fast Growing Treescould prove just as appealing to nesting hummingbirds as it does owls), while natural vegetation can help support the small mammals that owls feed on.

Don't worry; you really don't need to let the whole yard run wild (as Justin Bieber's near-immaculate garden proves) – even a small corner can help support local wildlife.

Owls are particularly active around dusk and (duh!) during the night, so creating a peaceful and naturally dark environment can help make your yard more welcoming. Consider switching off unnecessary outdoor lights, using motion-sensor lighting where needed, and avoiding bright spotlights that illuminate trees and potential nesting areas throughout the night.

Basically, invest in the kind of garden lighting that reduces light pollution as a rule, and keep it off at night if you want to do your bit. And try, too, keeping noise and disturbance to a minimum around trees and nesting sites.

If you want an owl to visit your garden just as it did Justin Bieber's yard, then it's also important to think carefully about how you eliminate rats.

Rodenticides (rat and mouse poisons) can be dangerous to owls, which may become poisoned after eating contaminated critters. If you want to encourage these beautiful birds into your yard, avoid using rodent poisons, then, and instead opt for safer, more owl-friendly approaches to pest management instead.

If you, like Justin Bieber, are lucky enough to spot an owl in your garden, take care to admire it from a distance rather than approaching or shining a light towards it (and consider investing in a Solar Trail Camera like this one to get your photos). After all, the idea isn't to persuade an owl to become a regular garden guest at any cost, but to create an outdoor space where local wildlife can thrive.

And while there's no guarantee that making these changes will result in an owl visit, you might just find that your garden becomes a little more appealing to some of nature's most fascinating nighttime visitors.

As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

#8200. Ask Dr. Paola – HELP! My Orphaned Kittens Are Suckling Each Other! (October 19, 2026)

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their cat's health and well-being. Whether you're a new pet parent or a seasoned cat lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral issues, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your kitty happy, healthy, and feline fine. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your cat, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your furry companion. â

Our four kittens â one female, three males â lost their mommy just after they turned two months old. They were already raiding her food bowl to munch on her dry kibble. Since mommy passed away from mastitis, they have developed a habit of trying to suckle on one another. I have seen each kitten do this.

We tried to separate them as soon as we see them doing this, but nothing works.

I am so sorry these babies lost their mama so suddenly. They have essentially decided, âNo Mom? Fine, weâll improvise!â

What you are seeing is called non-nutritive suckling, and in orphaned kittens, it can be surprisingly persistent. It is not necessarily hunger at this age. Suckling is also a built-in comfort behavior, and losing their mother can leave them looking for another way to satisfy that need. Research in orphaned kittens has specifically documented cross-suckling between littermates, with a higher risk in kittens that lost their mother.

Rather than simply trying to stop the behavior, you could give them an appropriate place to redirect it. There has been research into providing a âsurrogate motherâ for orphaned kittens, essentially a soft plush object fitted with artificial nipples, sometimes described as a kitten pacifier or nursing station. The idea is lovely because it gives them an outlet for that very normal suckling drive while allowing the siblings to continue enjoying their important social contact. I would look for a purpose-designed kitten nursing surrogate or a very soft, durable, washable object specifically intended for this use, rather than improvising with anything that could shed fibers, unravel, or be swallowed.

It is also worth knowing that some cats never completely give up their âbaby habit.â Suckling can persist into adulthood and may be directed toward blankets, clothing, plastics, themselves, siblings, or other cats, and even towards the owners. In many cats, it is simply a comforting ritual, but it becomes a concern if they chew and swallow fabric or fur, or if another cat develops irritated or injured skin. So for these four little characters, the goal does not necessarily have to be âstop suckling forever.â It is more about teaching them, âHere is your approved place to do that.â

Most importantly, keep an eye on the areas they are currently targeting. Suckling around the belly or especially the genital area can cause significant irritation and injury, so those kittens should be separated from the suckler when necessary and examined for redness, swelling, hair loss, wounds, or difficulty urinating.

With a safe alternative, plenty of play and enrichment, and gentle redirection, they may gradually outgrow the behavior, or they may simply become those adult cats who still insist on having their favorite comfort blanket. Some cats do have a talent for keeping their childhood traditions!

Black-eyed Susan (Rudbeckia spp.) is a popular native perennial, loved for its cheerful, daisy-like flowers with bright yellow petals and contrasting dark centers. As a native flower, this perennial is generally easy to grow, especially once established in the right conditions

One aspect of black-eyed Susan care that can be confusing for gardeners is pruning. Should you deadhead the flowers? Should you cut plants back all the way in winter? How do you trim black-eyed Susans? The answers to these questions, and more, depend on your goals, the time of year, and the types of Rudbeckia.

In our expert guide, we explain when and how to trim and prune black-eyed Susan and answer gardeners’ most frequently asked questions. Careful and timely pruning will keep your plants healthy and coming back year after year.

The timing for pruning black-eyed Susan depends on the reason for doing so. There are a few opportunities throughout the year:

Even within these parameters, gardeners have some wiggle room. You don’t have to deadhead, for instance. You also don’t have to cut back healthy plants just because the growing season has come to an end.

Exactly how you’ll cut back your plants depends on the specific task, but these are general best practices for routine pruning:

Trim off any diseased-looking plant material whenever you see it and dispose of it in the waste, not compost.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Deadheading is one of the most useful pruning chores gardeners have at their disposal. Selective removal of spent flowers keeps perennials like black-eyed Susans flowering until seasonal and weather changes start to trigger dormancy.

Remove spent flowers once the petals fade and drop off, or whenever they no longer look tidy or at their peak. Cut the stem under the flower back to the next healthy leaf or side bud.

You can also accompany summer deadheading with a light overall trim if the plant is looking leggy. Trim stems back to side buds or the base, but do so carefully and selectively. Avoid heavy pruning in summer.

As long as the plant looks healthy, you can keep your black-eyed Susan standing in fall and through winter. The standing seedheads provide valuable food for birds in winter and offer some visual interest in winter beds. The plants also provide shelter for beneficial insects.

If your plants don’t look healthy, for instance if you see signs of fungal disease, it’s best to cut them back. Cut all the stems and foliage back to the ground and dispose of it. Don’t put it in the compost pile, as this can spread disease.

You can also cut back plants if you prefer a tidier appearance in winter. This can also help you prevent self-seeding if you don’t want your black-eyed Susans to spread.

Pruning needs are generally similar across types, but there are a few considerations for different black-eyed Susans:

Deadheading black-eyed Susans encourages more blooming in the same season. Severely cutting back the plant before it has gone dormant can reduce blooming. Cutting back before winter will not restrict next year’s flowers.

For deadheading, cut back to the next healthy leaf or side bud. For seasonal cut-backs, trim stems all the way down to the ground.

Deadheading is optional, but plants should be cut back all the way either in late fall before winter or in spring before or just as new growth emerges.

Not necessarily. Leaving native perennials in place over winter supports wildlife and offers some visual interest in garden beds. The exception is diseased plants. These should be cut back.

Black-eyed Susan pruning is actually pretty simple. Deadhead in summer to enjoy more flowers and cut back spent material before winter or in early spring. The choice is yours and depends on your preferences, type of plant, and whether or not you support native wildlife.

#8198. 48 Bulldogs, One Apartment, and a Disturbing Secret

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

This is exactly why we are against puppy mills.

Forty-eight dogs â mostly French Bulldogs and English Bulldogs â found in what authorities are describing as a clandestine breeding operation in San Juan de Miraflores, Peru.

And when you read what was found, it is hard not to feel angry.

Authorities discovered the animals in appalling conditions on September 28 in an apartment on JirÃ³n Santiago RodrÃ­guez. The group included 25 French Bulldogs, nine English Bulldogs, eight mixed-breed dogs, five French Bulldog puppies, and one Dachshund. There was also a rooster. Local French Bulldog club, Club Frenchie, heard about the rescue through social media and immediately reached out to offer assistance. One member of the club spoke to a reporter from the Peruvian newspaper El Comercio about what they had witnessed:

âThe state of health was absolutely deplorable. There were dogs covered in feces, filthy, with no hygiene whatsoever, dogs with broken nails, bitten ears, and other serious problems,â he said.

The dogs were brought to the Municipal Veterinary Clinic in San Juan de Miraflores, where they were examined and received treatment for a range of conditions. Most were suffering from heat stress, and many had excessively long nails, some bleeding, skin problems, fungal issues, eye infections, surgical scars, and other conditions requiring medical attention. Six puppies reportedly needed incubator care, with two described as being in a particularly fragile condition.

Following the intervention, the animals were taken to the municipal veterinary service, and some have since been moved into foster care. The San Juan de Miraflores Provincial Corporate Criminal Prosecutor's Office is investigating the case, and FÃ©lix Sonco and Darlys Vanegas were arrested at the scene.

As if the horrendous conditions that greeted rescuers werenât disturbing enough, it appears that this wasnât simply a breeding operation, but an illegal, makeshift veterinary clinic.

Some of these dogs had undergone surgery on their vocal cords; a barbaric procedure known as debarking. Being kept in cramped and filthy conditions meant that these dogs were barking and crying constantly. Debarking was a way to reduce noise and avoid complaints.

They didnât improve conditions. They didnât provide relief. They simply removed their ability to voice their distress.

Evidence also suggests that several female Bulldogs were bred repeatedly, with some reportedly forced to carry as many as ten litters of puppies. Veterinary examination also found evidence that crude cesarean surgeries had been performed prematurely to get puppies out faster and back on the market, while the mothers, if they survived, were bred again.

Investigators reportedly found premature newborn puppies inside an unsterilized incubator, while puppies were being sold for around 1,500 to 2,500 Peruvian soles each â roughly $400 to $670 USD.

French Bulldogs and English Bulldogs are brachycephalic breeds. Their shortened skull and squishy faces are a big part of their appeal. But there is a very uncomfortable truth behind that cute face.

That same anatomy that many people find irresistible can make it harder for a dog to breathe, exercise, sleep, regulate their body temperature, and, in some cases, give birth.

We have to stop pretending these things are simply âpart of being a Bulldog.â

A dog struggling to breathe is not just a snorer. A dog that overheats easily is not just âsensitive to the heat.â These are medical problems.

Brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome (BOAS) refers to the conditions that affect breeds with a shortened skull, or âbrachycephaly.â These conditions include hypoplastic trachea (narrow  windpipe), stenotic nares (narrow nostrils), and a tongue and soft palate that are too large and long for the mouth, resulting in obstruction of the airways and difficulty swallowing.

These issues have led many veterinary professionals and animal welfare advocates to question the ethics of breeding these dogs. When a physical characteristic can affect basic functions like breathing and temperature regulation, choosing which dogs reproduce needs to consider more than appearance.

That little flat face. Those big eyes. The stout little body. The funny little snorts.

Most people see cute, even adorable. But as veterinarians, we see a whole list of problems that need to be monitored.

A Bulldog can be an absolutely wonderful companion and still have anatomy that puts them at risk for serious health problems. Breeding of these dogs should require more responsibility, not less, with breeders selecting for less extreme conformations.

There is something very sad about how much importance we place on how dogs look. A certain face. A certain size. A certain coat. A certain breed.

The more desirable that look becomes, the more money there is in producing it. That creates a market, and unfortunately, where there is money, there will always be those willing to cut corners.

This does not mean that every breeder is bad. There are responsible breeders who health-test their dogs, carefully select breeding pairs, provide appropriate veterinary care, and take responsibility for the puppies they bring into the world. Those who are actively trying to breed healthier versions of dogs whose health and function have been crippled through selective breeding for exaggerated features.

Puppy mills are something very different.

The problem is when the animals producing those puppies become a means to an end.

And veterinary care becomes an expense to minimize or avoid, not an essential part of responsible animal care.

When it comes to looking for your next four-legged family member, start your search at an animal shelter. Research your favorite breed and know how to recognize a suspicious situation.

If you are planning to purchase or adopt a puppy, you should be able to inspect the home or facility where the puppy was raised, and meet the puppyâs mother. Breeders who are unwilling or unable to allow this raise suspicions of unethical practice, and if you are concerned about a potential welfare issue, donât be tempted to buy a puppy to ârescueâ it â this simply finances the operation. Instead, contact your local animal control agency, humane society, sheriff, or police department.

When extreme conformation interferes with breathing and thermoregulation, when it increases the risk of difficult births and chronic airway problems, we need to consider whether breeding these dogs is the right thing to do. But if people will buy them, people will breed them.

Itâs up to us to look past the adorable face we saw on Instagram and ask:

And, as the horrific plight of these 48 dogs reminds us, where did they come from?

The problem is loving an appearance so much that we stop asking what that appearance means for the animal.

These dogs have been through a terrible situation, but now they have a chance.

They need veterinary care. Their nails need treatment, their skin and eyes need evaluation, their nutritional needs need to be addressed, and their other medical problems need to be properly investigated. Some require specialized treatment, while others are recovering in foster homes.

And hopefully, many of these dogs will eventually experience something that should have been completely ordinary from the beginning:

These dogs were not born to produce puppies. They were not born to be quiet. They were not born to look a certain way for someone else's profit.

For that reason, adoption should always be considered before buying a puppy.

There are so many wonderful dogs already waiting in shelters, foster homes, and recovering from neglect. Dogs that may not have the perfect face or pedigree but have an enormous capacity to love.

Please, before asking where to buy the puppy with the cutest face, ask who is already waiting for someone to choose them.

Dr. Paola Cuevas is our Senior In-House Veterinarian at Dogster and Pangolia. She has over 19 years of experience working with an array of species and loves sharing her knowledge and experience with our readers and aims to provide assistance with any issue presented by your non-human family members. She received her degree from the University of Guadalajara, Mexico.

Her passions are animal welfare and preventive medicine, and has skills in the fields of nutrition, microscopy, clinical pathology, diagnostic imaging, and endoscopy. Paola frequently contributes pet care insight to various media outlets like PetMD, The Daily Record, Parents.com, etc.

Paola is also an animal behaviorist with extensive experience in positive reinforcement animal training.
